questions.text: Endoparasite is a term applied to:
questions.explanation: Endoparasites live inside the host, either in tissues or body cavities/lumens, so their presence is described as infection rather than surface infestation. Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host, and obligatory/facultative terms describe dependence on the host, not location.
questions.keyConcept: Endoparasite = parasite living inside the host → infection.
options: A parasite that lives within its host and said to cause infection
A parasite that lives on the outer surface of its host

questions.text: Ectoparasite is:
questions.explanation: Ectoparasites remain on the external surface of the host, such as skin or hair, so they are classically associated with infestation. Endoparasites live internally, while “obligatory” and “facultative” describe whether the parasite can survive without parasitism.
questions.keyConcept: Ectoparasite = surface-dwelling parasite → infestation.
options: A parasite that lives on the outer surface of host (infection)

questions.text: Temporary parasite is a parasite that :
questions.explanation: Temporary parasites contact the host only intermittently, usually to obtain a blood meal, then leave the host environment. This differs from permanent parasites, which remain on or in the host for most of their life cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Temporary parasites visit the host only for feeding.
options: Lives on the outer surface of the host
Lives within its host and is said to cause infestation
Visits the hosts from time to time for meals

questions.text: Obligatory parasite
questions.explanation: An obligatory parasite is metabolically or biologically dependent on the host and cannot normally complete its life cycle as a free-living organism. Facultative parasites can alternate between free-living and parasitic existence, so they are not fully host-dependent.
questions.keyConcept: Obligatory parasite = must live parasitically to survive/complete its cycle.
options: Can change their life style free living and parasitic life
Is completely dependent upon the host
Visit the hosts from time to time
Capable of producing disease in immuno-compromised person

questions.text: Facultative parasite:
questions.explanation: A facultative parasite can live independently but may become parasitic under suitable conditions. This is important clinically because some normally free-living organisms can invade compromised hosts or tissues and produce disease.
questions.keyConcept: Facultative parasite = free-living organism capable of parasitism.
options: Can change its life cycle from free-living to parasitic
Transmitted from animal to animal only

questions.text: Dead end infection is:
questions.explanation: A dead-end host permits infection but does not allow the parasite to continue transmission or complete its normal life cycle. The parasite may cause disease in that host, but the host is epidemiologically unhelpful for maintaining the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Dead-end infection = parasite cannot complete/transmit its life cycle from that host.
options: End by death of the human
End by the death of animal
Parasite cannot complete its life cycle
End by death of the intermediate host

questions.text: Definitive host is the host that carries:
questions.explanation: The definitive host harbors the adult or sexually mature stage of a parasite, and sexual reproduction occurs there when present. Intermediate hosts carry larval or asexual stages, while reservoir hosts maintain infection in nature.
questions.keyConcept: Definitive host = adult/sexually mature parasite stage.
options: Sexually mature adult stage of the parasite
Same parasitic stage that may found in human
Sexually immature stages of the parasite

questions.text: Intermediate host is the host that carries:
questions.explanation: An intermediate host carries the immature, larval, or asexual developmental stage of the parasite. This contrasts with the definitive host, which carries the mature adult or sexual stage.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate host = larval/immature/asexual parasite stage.
options: Sexually mature stages of the parasite
Same parasitic stages like those found in human
Sexually immature larval stages of the parasite

questions.text: Reservoir host
questions.explanation: A reservoir host is an animal source that maintains the same infective parasite stage found in humans and helps preserve transmission in nature. It is different from a vector, which transmits the parasite, and from an intermediate host, which supports larval development.
questions.keyConcept: Reservoir host = animal maintenance source of human-infective stages.
options: Animal that carries same parasitic stages like those found in human
is an arthropod that carries & transmits dieases from host to another
Is the host in which the larval stage of the parasite remains viable without further development
Human containg larval stages which infect human

questions.text: Human containing an adult worm in the small intestine acts as a ___ host; the parasite is an ___ parasite and is ___ because it cannot live without the host
questions.explanation: This fill-in item tests exact parasitology terminology rather than recall of a long option list. Each blank changes the biological meaning: host type defines where development occurs, parasite location defines infection versus infestation, and dependency defines whether the organism is obligatory or facultative.
questions.keyConcept: Use exact terminology: host type, parasite location, and dependency are separate concepts.

questions.text: Monoxenous parasite is:
questions.explanation: A monoxenous parasite completes its entire life cycle in one host, so no intermediate host is required. Heteroxenous parasites require more than one host, which is why their control often depends on interrupting host-to-host transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Monoxenous = one-host life cycle.
options: Parasite in which life cycle occurs in one host only
Parasite in which multiply by sexual reproduction only
Parasite in which life cycle need one intermediate host only
Parasite in which multiply by asexual reproduction only

questions.text: Heteroxenous parasite is
questions.explanation: A heteroxenous parasite requires more than one host to complete its life cycle, usually a definitive host plus one or more intermediate hosts. This is a key transmission concept because disease control may target either the human host, animal reservoir, vector, or intermediate host.
questions.keyConcept: Heteroxenous = indirect life cycle needing more than one host.
options: Parasite which multiply sexually followed by asexually multiplication
Parasite in which life cycle need at least two intermediate host
Parasite have a indirect life cycle
All of the above with intermediate

questions.text: Trematoda have
questions.explanation: Trematodes are flatworms with an incomplete digestive tract, typically two blind intestinal caeca and no anus. Cestodes lack an alimentary canal, while nematodes have a complete digestive tract with separate mouth and anus.
questions.keyConcept: Trematodes: incomplete gut with blind caeca and no anus.
options: Incomplete alimentary canal (2 blind intestinal caeca) without anal pore =
With well developed oesophagus as Nematoda
Without alimentary canal as in Cestoda

questions.text: Trematodes have mostly :
questions.explanation: Most trematodes possess oral and ventral suckers that help attachment to host tissues. Genital suckers are not the usual defining pair, and cestodes instead use a scolex with suckers or bothria depending on the order.
questions.keyConcept: Trematodes are classically recognized by oral and ventral suckers.

questions.text: Hermaphrodites (monoecious) can do:
questions.explanation: Most trematodes and cestodes are hermaphroditic, allowing self-fertilization, cross-fertilization, or both depending on the parasite and circumstances. Schistosomes are the important exception among trematodes because they have separate male and female worms.
questions.keyConcept: Hermaphroditic helminths can perform self- and/or cross-fertilization; schistosomes are dioecious.

questions.text: All Trematoda eggs are:
questions.explanation: Trematode eggs are mainly diagnostic stages because they are detected in stool, urine, sputum, or tissue depending on the species. The infective stage for humans is usually metacercaria, except schistosomes where cercariae actively penetrate skin.
questions.keyConcept: Trematode eggs are generally diagnostic, not the human infective stage.

questions.text: The stage that enters the snail in the life cycle of the Trematoda is/are
questions.explanation: The miracidium is the trematode larva that infects the snail intermediate host after hatching from the egg. Some species have eggs containing miracidia that are ingested by the snail, but the biologic principle remains that the miracidial stage initiates snail infection.
questions.keyConcept: Miracidium is the trematode stage that infects the snail.
options: Eggs containing miracidium as in Heterophyes (doesn't need snail)

questions.text: Which of the following larval stages is not always present in life cycle of Trematoda:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Redia. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Which of the following larval stages is not always present in life cycle of Trematoda: → Redia.

questions.text: A ciliated conical organism which comes out from the hatched egg in Trematoda is
questions.explanation: The miracidium is the ciliated larval stage that hatches from many trematode eggs and seeks the snail intermediate host. Its cilia enable active swimming in water, which distinguishes it from sporocyst, redia, and cercaria.
questions.keyConcept: Miracidium = ciliated trematode larva that infects the snail.

questions.text: All the Cercaria arise from the snail developed to encysted metacercaria except:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes are transmitted by furcocercous cercariae, which leave the snail and actively penetrate human skin. This differs from most other trematodes, where humans acquire infection by ingesting encysted metacercariae on plants, fish, or crustaceans.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma infective stage = free-swimming furcocercous cercaria.

questions.text: In Trematoda life cycle, the stage that arises from the snail is: sucker
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cercaria. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: In Trematoda life cycle, the stage that arises from the snail is: sucker → Cercaria.

questions.explanation: The correct answer is All Trematoda eggs hatch to release miracidium in water. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The mode of infection of all Trematoda is ingestion except Schistosoma
All Trematoda eggs hatch to release miracidium in water
All Trematoda need snail as IH except heterophyes need snail & sh

questions.text: The cercaria arising from the snail & attached to the vegetable is :
questions.explanation: Fasciola-type leptocercous cercariae leave the snail and encyst as metacercariae on aquatic vegetation. Ingestion of contaminated plants then transmits the infection to humans or herbivores.
questions.keyConcept: Leptocercous cercariae encyst on aquatic plants in Fasciola-type cycles.

questions.text: The cercaria which arises from the snail & penetrate fish muscle to encyst is
questions.explanation: Lophocercous cercariae encyst in fish tissues as metacercariae in intestinal or liver fluke life cycles. This explains why eating raw or undercooked fish can transmit certain trematode infections.
questions.keyConcept: Fish-borne trematodes use lophocercous cercariae that encyst in fish.

questions.text: The cercaria with tail covered by membrane is
questions.explanation: Lophocercous cercariae have a tail with a fin-like membranous expansion. Leptocercous cercariae have a simple tail, while furcocercous cercariae have a forked tail as in schistosomes.
questions.keyConcept: Lophocercous cercaria = membranous tail.

questions.text: Leptocercus cercaria is:
questions.explanation: Leptocercous cercariae are defined by a simple, unforked tail. This distinguishes them from furcocercous cercariae with forked tails and lophocercous cercariae with membranous tails.
questions.keyConcept: Leptocercous cercaria = simple tail.

questions.text: Encysted metacercaria is the infective stage of all trematodes except:
questions.explanation: Encysted metacercaria is the usual infective stage for food-borne trematodes such as Fasciola, Heterophyes, and Paragonimus. Schistosoma is the exception because its cercariae do not encyst for ingestion; they penetrate intact skin.
questions.keyConcept: Most trematodes infect by metacercariae; Schistosoma infects by cercariae.

questions.text: Cestodes are characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Cestodes are flat, segmented, hermaphroditic worms with no functional digestive tract; they absorb nutrients through the tegument. Rostellum and hooks may be present in some species, but absence of an alimentary canal and segmentation are core cestode features.
questions.keyConcept: Cestodes = segmented flatworms lacking an alimentary canal.

questions.text: Neck of a cestodes is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The neck of a cestode is the germinal growth zone that produces new proglottids by strobilization. Therefore, it is responsible for segment/proglottid formation and continued elongation of the worm.
questions.keyConcept: Cestode neck = growth zone for strobilization and proglottid formation.

questions.text: Cestodes which have almond-shape scolex are:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Order Pseudophyllidea. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Cestodes which have almond-shape scolex are: → Order Pseudophyllidea.

questions.text: Common genital pore in the ventral surface of

questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Common genital pore in the ventral surface of → Order Pseudophyllidae.

questions.text: Cestodes which have blind uterus:
questions.explanation: Cyclophyllidean cestodes characteristically have a blind uterus, lateral genital pores, compact vitelline glands, and eggs containing a hexacanth embryo. Pseudophyllideans instead have operculated eggs and a uterine pore.
questions.keyConcept: Cyclophyllidea = blind uterus + lateral genital pore + hexacanth eggs.

questions.text: The operculated eggs is or are the eggs of
questions.explanation: Pseudophyllidean cestodes have operculated eggs and solid larvae such as procercoid and plerocercoid stages. This contrasts with cyclophyllidean eggs, which are thick-shelled and contain a hexacanth embryo.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudophyllidea = operculated eggs + procercoid/plerocercoid larvae.

questions.text: Order Cyclophyllidea eggs characterized by
questions.explanation: Cyclophyllidean cestodes characteristically have a blind uterus, lateral genital pores, compact vitelline glands, and eggs containing a hexacanth embryo. Pseudophyllideans instead have operculated eggs and a uterine pore.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about the general characters of Nematodes ?
questions.explanation: Nematodes are cylindrical, unsegmented, dioecious worms with a body wall formed by cuticle, hypodermis, and longitudinal muscles. Saying the male usually has an anal opening is inaccurate because the male posterior opening is typically a cloaca, not a simple anus.
questions.keyConcept: Nematodes are cylindrical dioecious worms; male posterior opening is a cloaca.
options: The body wall is composed of 3 layers
The male usually has anal opening

questions.text: Body of nematodes is formed of:
questions.explanation: The nematode body wall consists of cuticle, hypodermis, and longitudinal muscle layers. These layers give nematodes their cylindrical shape and characteristic movement, unlike flatworms which are dorsoventrally flattened.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode body wall = cuticle + hypodermis + longitudinal muscles.

questions.text: Regarding size and posterior end, nematode male is:
questions.explanation: Male nematodes are usually smaller than females and often have a ventrally curved posterior end for copulation. They do not have two female reproductive systems, and absence of muscle is not a nematode feature.
questions.keyConcept: Male nematodes are typically smaller with a ventrally curved posterior end.

questions.text: The muscular oesophagus with triradiate lumen is/ are
questions.explanation: The correct answer is All of the above. This item tests nematode morphology, reproduction, or larval development. Nematodes are dioecious cylindrical worms with a complete gut and stage-specific larval morphology, which separates them from trematodes and cestodes.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode high-yield point: The muscular oesophagus with triradiate lumen is/ are → All of the above.

questions.text: Filarial worms is/ are
questions.explanation: The correct answer is All of the above. This item tests nematode morphology, reproduction, or larval development. Nematodes are dioecious cylindrical worms with a complete gut and stage-specific larval morphology, which separates them from trematodes and cestodes.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode high-yield point: Filarial worms is/ are → All of the above.
options: The have cylindrical oesophagus cylindrical a

questions.text: Regarding genitalia, nematode male has:
questions.explanation: Male nematodes have a single reproductive tract and copulatory spicules that help transfer sperm. Females may be monodelphic or didelphic, but two genital systems is a female-pattern concept, not a male one.
questions.keyConcept: Male nematode = single genital tract with copulatory spicules.
options: Has one set of genitalia with copulatory spicules

questions.text: Nematodes can do:
questions.explanation: Nematodes are dioecious with separate male and female worms, so reproduction requires cross-fertilization. This is different from many trematodes and cestodes, which are hermaphroditic.
questions.keyConcept: Nematodes are dioecious → cross-fertilization only.

questions.text: Viviparous nematode female passes:
questions.explanation: Viviparous nematode females release larvae rather than eggs after fertilization. This is different from oviparous females that lay eggs and ovoviviparous females that release eggs already containing larvae.
questions.keyConcept: Viviparous nematodes release larvae directly after fertilization, not eggs.
options: Pass immature eggs contain ovum or cells after fertilization
Pass mature eggs contain larva that immediately hatch after fertilization

questions.text: A tissue nematode female with two sets of genital organs is sexually ___
questions.explanation: This fill-in item tests exact parasitology terminology rather than recall of a long option list. Each blank changes the biological meaning: host type defines where development occurs, parasite location defines infection versus infestation, and dependency defines whether the organism is obligatory or facultative.
questions.keyConcept: Use exact terminology: host type, parasite location, and dependency are separate concepts.

questions.text: Number of nematode larvae in life cycle are:
questions.explanation: Nematodes pass through four larval stages before becoming adults. The infective stage is often the third-stage larva, but the universal life-cycle structure includes L1 through L4.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode life cycle has four larval stages.

questions.text: The 1" larva in life cycle of nematodes has:
questions.explanation: The first-stage nematode larva classically has a rhabditiform oesophagus, especially in intestinal nematode development. Filariform oesophagus is more typical of the infective third-stage larva.
questions.keyConcept: L1 nematode larva = rhabditiform oesophagus.

questions.text: The 3rd larva & usually the infective stage in life cycle of nematodes has:
questions.explanation: The third-stage nematode larva is commonly the infective stage and typically has a filariform oesophagus. This contrasts with the first-stage rhabditiform larva used in diagnostic morphology.
questions.keyConcept: Infective L3 nematode larva = filariform oesophagus.

questions.text: Rhizopodes (Sarcodina or ameba) are protozoa that move by which of the following methods?
questions.explanation: Rhizopodes, also called amoebae, move by pseudopodia formed by cytoplasmic extension. Cilia and flagella are locomotor organs of other protozoal groups, while microtubule-based gliding is associated with apicomplexans.
questions.keyConcept: Rhizopoda/Sarcodina amoebae move by pseudopodia, not cilia or flagella.

questions.text: Sporozoa (Apicomplexa) moves by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Apicomplexans do not rely on cilia or flagella for ordinary locomotion; they use microtubule-associated gliding mechanisms and an apical complex for invasion. This is clinically relevant for parasites such as Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
questions.keyConcept: Apicomplexa use microtubule-based gliding/invasion machinery.

questions.text: What is the axoneme ?
questions.explanation: The axoneme is the intracytoplasmic axial filament/core of a flagellum or cilium and contains the microtubular apparatus responsible for movement. The external free portion is supported by this internal axonemal structure.
questions.keyConcept: Axoneme = internal microtubular core of flagellum/cilium.

questions.text: Class Zoomastigophora move by
questions.explanation: Zoomastigophora are flagellated protozoa, so flagella are their main locomotor organ. Amoebae use pseudopodia, ciliates use cilia, and apicomplexans generally lack obvious locomotor organelles.
questions.keyConcept: Zoomastigophora are flagellated protozoa; flagella are their defining locomotor organelles.

questions.text: Endocytosis through micropores occurs by which of the following protozoa?
questions.explanation: Sporozoa/Apicomplexa take in nutrients through micropores and specialized surface structures rather than by amoeboid phagocytosis. This reflects their highly adapted intracellular or tissue-parasitic lifestyle.
questions.keyConcept: Apicomplexa use micropores for endocytosis/nutrition.

questions.text: What is the inactive form with resistant wall that may be found protozoa?
questions.explanation: The cyst is a resistant, inactive stage that survives unfavorable environmental conditions and often serves as the infective form. Trophozoites are active, motile, feeding forms and are usually less environmentally resistant.
questions.keyConcept: Protozoan cyst = resistant/infective dormant stage.

questions.text: Phylum Apicomplexa are protozoa is characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Apicomplexa characteristically have complex life cycles with both asexual multiplication and sexual reproduction. This combination explains why many apicomplexan infections involve different stages in human and vector or definitive hosts.
questions.keyConcept: Apicomplexa reproduce both asexually and sexually.

questions.text: Class Ciliata (Balantidium) are protozoa is characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ciliates such as Balantidium move by cilia and can reproduce sexually by conjugation. Schizogony and sporogony are more typical of apicomplexans, not ciliates.
questions.keyConcept: Balantidium/Ciliata are ciliated protozoa and may reproduce sexually by conjugation.

questions.text: The Arthopoda having body which have divided body into head, thorax & abdomen and 3 pairs of legs, belongs to class
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Insecta. The item is testing a core parasitology definition, and the correct option fits the biologic meaning of the stem rather than merely sounding related. The distractors are adjacent concepts from other parasite groups, host categories, or transmission patterns.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield point: The Arthopoda having body which have divided body into head, thorax & abdomen and 3 pairs of legs, belongs to class → Insecta.

questions.text: The Class of Arthropoda which having 2 pairs of antenna belongs to
questions.explanation: Two pairs of antennae are characteristic of maxillopod/crustacean-type arthropods rather than insects or arachnids. Insects have one pair of antennae, and arachnids have no antennae.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillopoda/crustaceans = two pairs of antennae.

questions.text: The Class of Arthropoda which having 4 pairs of legs & no antenna belongs to :
questions.explanation: Arachnids have four pairs of legs and lack antennae, which separates them from insects. This group includes ticks and mites, important vectors and causes of ectoparasitic disease.
questions.keyConcept: Arachnida = 4 pairs of legs and no antennae.

questions.text: Complete metamorphosis is done by all the following arthropods except:
questions.explanation: Complete metamorphosis includes egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages, as seen in mosquitoes, flies, and fleas. Lice undergo incomplete metamorphosis and lack a pupal stage, making them the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Lice have incomplete metamorphosis; mosquitoes/flies/fleas have complete metamorphosis.

questions.text: if the arthropoda transmit the organism by inoculation without any change in morphology or number, this is called :
questions.explanation: Mechanical transmission means the vector carries the pathogen without multiplication or developmental change. Biological transmission requires parasite multiplication, development, or both inside the vector.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanical transmission = no development and no multiplication in the vector.

questions.text: if the organism (helminths) changes in morphology only inside the insects during transmission, this is called
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cyclodevelopmental transmission. The item is testing a core parasitology definition, and the correct option fits the biologic meaning of the stem rather than merely sounding related. The distractors are adjacent concepts from other parasite groups, host categories, or transmission patterns.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield point: if the organism (helminths) changes in morphology only inside the insects during transmission, this is called → Cyclodevelopmental transmission.

questions.text: if the organism (protozoa) changes in number and morphology inside the insects during transmission, this is called
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cyclopropagative. The item is testing a core parasitology definition, and the correct option fits the biologic meaning of the stem rather than merely sounding related. The distractors are adjacent concepts from other parasite groups, host categories, or transmission patterns.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield point: if the organism (protozoa) changes in number and morphology inside the insects during transmission, this is called → Cyclopropagative.

questions.text: Type of transmission of malaria Inside mosquitoes is:
questions.explanation: Malaria parasites undergo both multiplication and developmental transformation in the mosquito, so the transmission is cyclopropagative. This distinguishes it from purely mechanical carriage or cyclodevelopment without multiplication.
questions.keyConcept: Malaria in mosquito = cyclopropagative transmission.

questions.text: Type of transmission of viruses & bacteria inside arthropods is:
questions.explanation: Many arboviruses and bacteria multiply inside arthropods without the complex developmental metamorphosis seen in protozoa or helminths. This is propagative transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Propagative transmission = multiplication in vector without developmental change.

questions.text: Transovarian transmission is found in:
questions.explanation: Transovarian transmission occurs when an infected arthropod passes the pathogen to its eggs and offspring. Ticks are classic examples, helping maintain infection across vector generations.
questions.keyConcept: Transovarian transmission is classically seen in ticks.

questions.text: All trematodes are hermaphrodite except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Schistosoma species. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: All trematodes are hermaphrodite except: → Schistosoma species.

The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.

questions.text: Choose the incorrect blend:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Procercoid / Nematode. This item tests nematode morphology, reproduction, or larval development. Nematodes are dioecious cylindrical worms with a complete gut and stage-specific larval morphology, which separates them from trematodes and cestodes.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode high-yield point: Choose the incorrect blend: → Procercoid / Nematode.
options: Sporocyst / Trematode. - 1 - him Parasitology - Infection - MCQ Dr Ayman

questions.text: The larval stage that comes out from snail in life cycle of trematodes is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cercaria. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: The larval stage that comes out from snail in life cycle of trematodes is: → Cercaria.

questions.text: ™ Plathelminthes are flat except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Schistosoma females. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: ™ Plathelminthes are flat except: → Schistosoma females.

questions.text: Hermaphrodites can do:
questions.explanation: Most trematodes and cestodes are hermaphroditic, allowing self-fertilization, cross-fertilization, or both depending on the parasite and circumstances. Schistosomes are the important exception among trematodes because they have separate male and female worms.
questions.keyConcept: Hermaphroditic helminths can perform self- and/or cross-fertilization; schistosomes are dioecious.

questions.text: Schistosomes can do:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes have separate male and female worms, so reproduction requires cross-fertilization rather than self-fertilization. This is a major exception to the usual hermaphroditic pattern of trematodes.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosomes are dioecious trematodes → cross-fertilization only.

questions.text: The ciliated larva of trematodes is:
questions.explanation: The miracidium is the ciliated larval stage that hatches from many trematode eggs and seeks the snail intermediate host. Its cilia enable active swimming in water, which distinguishes it from sporocyst, redia, and cercaria.
questions.keyConcept: Miracidium = ciliated trematode larva that infects the snail.

questions.text: The infective stage of schistosomes is:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes are transmitted by furcocercous cercariae, which leave the snail and actively penetrate human skin. This differs from most other trematodes, where humans acquire infection by ingesting encysted metacercariae on plants, fish, or crustaceans.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma infective stage = free-swimming furcocercous cercaria.

questions.text: Eggs of trematodes are operculated except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Schistosomes. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Eggs of trematodes are operculated except: → Schistosomes.

questions.text: Larval stage of trematodes which is not found in schistosomes is:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes lack the redia stage and develop in the snail through sporocyst generations before producing cercariae. This is one reason schistosome life cycles differ from many other trematodes.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosome life cycle lacks redia.

questions.text: Cercaria with membranous tail is:
questions.explanation: Lophocercous cercariae have a tail with a fin-like membranous expansion. Leptocercous cercariae have a simple tail, while furcocercous cercariae have a forked tail as in schistosomes.
questions.keyConcept: Lophocercous cercaria = membranous tail.

questions.text: All trematodes are transmitted to by ingestion except:
questions.explanation: Most trematodes infect humans by ingestion of metacercariae in aquatic plants, fish, or crustaceans. Schistosomes are the exception because their cercariae penetrate skin during water exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma transmission is skin penetration, not ingestion.

questions.text: Cestodes which have almond-shaped scolex are:
questions.explanation: Pseudophyllidean cestodes have an elongated or almond-shaped scolex with two bothria rather than four true suckers. Cyclophyllidean cestodes typically have four suckers and may have a rostellum or hooks.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudophyllidea = two bothria/almond-shaped scolex.

questions.text: Cestodes which have no gravid segment are:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Both a & b. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Cestodes which have no gravid segment are: → Both a & b.
options: Hymenolepis nana -4- Parasitology - Infection - MCQ. Dr Ayman

questions.text: Cestodes are:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Flat & segmented worms. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Cestodes are: → Flat & segmented worms.

questions.text: Cestodes which have 2 suckers:
questions.explanation: Pseudophyllidean cestodes have an elongated or almond-shaped scolex with two bothria rather than four true suckers. Cyclophyllidean cestodes typically have four suckers and may have a rostellum or hooks.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudophyllidea = two bothria/almond-shaped scolex.

questions.text: Nematode which can be transmitted by inhalation of
questions.explanation: Enterobius eggs are light and may become airborne, allowing inhalation or ingestion of infective eggs in contaminated environments. Hookworms infect mainly by skin penetration, while filarial worms require arthropod vectors.
questions.keyConcept: Enterobius infection can occur by inhalation/ingestion of infective eggs.

questions.text: The 3rd larva in the life cycle of nematodes has:
questions.explanation: The third-stage nematode larva is commonly the infective stage and typically has a filariform oesophagus. This contrasts with the first-stage rhabditiform larva used in diagnostic morphology.
questions.keyConcept: Infective L3 nematode larva = filariform oesophagus.

questions.text: All nematode females are didelphic except:
questions.explanation: A didelphic female has two sets of genital tubes, a common arrangement in many nematodes. Recognizing didelphic versus monodelphic females is useful for species identification in nematode morphology.
questions.keyConcept: Didelphic female = two female reproductive tubes.

questions.text: Regarding sex, nematodes are:
questions.explanation: Nematodes are dioecious, meaning male and female worms are separate. This is a major distinction from most cestodes and many trematodes, which are hermaphroditic.
questions.keyConcept: Nematodes are dioecious helminths with separate male and female worms.

questions.text: Regarding body shape, nematodes are:
questions.explanation: Nematodes are cylindrical, elongated, and non-segmented. Cestodes are flat and segmented, while trematodes are flat and unsegmented.
questions.keyConcept: Nematodes = cylindrical, non-segmented worms.

questions.text: Neck of a cestode worm is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The neck of a cestode is the germinal growth zone that produces new proglottids by strobilization. Therefore, it is responsible for segment/proglottid formation and continued elongation of the worm.
questions.keyConcept: Cestode neck = growth zone for strobilization and proglottid formation.

questions.text: Common genital pore is lateral in following cestodes:
questions.explanation: Cyclophyllidean cestodes characteristically have a blind uterus, lateral genital pores, compact vitelline glands, and eggs containing a hexacanth embryo. Pseudophyllideans instead have operculated eggs and a uterine pore.
questions.keyConcept: Cyclophyllidea = blind uterus + lateral genital pore + hexacanth eggs.

questions.text: Cestodes which have compact vitelline glands are:
questions.explanation: Cyclophyllidean cestodes characteristically have a blind uterus, lateral genital pores, compact vitelline glands, and eggs containing a hexacanth embryo. Pseudophyllideans instead have operculated eggs and a uterine pore.
questions.keyConcept: Cyclophyllidea = blind uterus + lateral genital pore + hexacanth eggs.

questions.text: The following are larval stages of cestodes except:
questions.explanation: Coracidium, procercoid, plerocercoid, cysticercus, cysticercoid, and hydatid forms are cestode-associated larval stages depending on the order. Miracidium belongs to trematodes, not cestodes, so it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Miracidium is a trematode larva, not a cestode larva.
options: Cysticercus -7- rahim Chiny parasitology - Infection - MCQ Dr Ayman

questions.text: Hydatid cyst is a cestode larva of:
questions.explanation: Hydatid cyst is a cystic larval stage of cyclophyllidean cestodes, classically Echinococcus. It is clinically important because expanding cysts can compress organs and rupture may trigger anaphylaxis or dissemination.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatid cyst = cyclophyllidean cestode larva, classically Echinococcus.

questions.text: Choose the correct blend:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Leptocercus cercaria / Simple tail. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Choose the correct blend: → Leptocercus cercaria / Simple tail.

questions.text: Ovoviviparous nematode female passes:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mature eggs containing larvae after fertilization. Ovoviviparous nematode females retain eggs until larval development has occurred, then pass embryonated eggs that may hatch soon after. This differs from oviparous females, which pass immature eggs, and viviparous females, which release larvae directly.
questions.keyConcept: Ovoviviparous nematodes pass mature embryonated eggs containing larvae.
options: Pass immature eggs contain ovum after fertilization
Pass mature eggs contain larva after fertilization

questions.text: All trematode eggs hatch to complete the life cycle in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Water. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: All trematode eggs hatch to complete the life cycle in: → Water.

questions.text: Cuticle of nematodes is secreted from:
questions.explanation: The nematode cuticle is secreted by the underlying hypodermis and is periodically shed during molting. This cuticle protects the worm and contributes to its characteristic body-wall structure.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode cuticle is secreted by the hypodermis.

questions.text: All the following are cystic cestode larvae except:
questions.explanation: Cysticercus, cysticercoid, and hydatid cyst are cystic larval forms associated mainly with cyclophyllidean cestodes. Procercoid is a solid larva, so it is not a cystic cestode larva.
questions.keyConcept: Cystic cestode larvae include cysticercus, cysticercoid, and hydatid cyst.

questions.text: Solid cestode larva:
questions.explanation: Procercoid is a solid cestode larval stage of pseudophyllidean tapeworms. In contrast, hydatid and cysticercus forms are cystic larvae, while miracidium, redia, and cercaria are trematode stages.
questions.keyConcept: Procercoid = solid pseudophyllidean cestode larva.

questions.text: Egg of Order Pseudophyllidea is:
questions.explanation: Pseudophyllidean cestodes have operculated eggs and solid larvae such as procercoid and plerocercoid stages. This contrasts with cyclophyllidean eggs, which are thick-shelled and contain a hexacanth embryo.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudophyllidea = operculated eggs + procercoid/plerocercoid larvae.

questions.text: Egg of Order Cyclophyllidea is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Contain hexacanth embryo. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Egg of Order Cyclophyllidea is: → Contain hexacanth embryo.

questions.text: Choose the correct worm morphology blend:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cestodes / Flat worms / Hermaphrodite. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Choose the correct worm morphology blend: → Cestodes / Flat worms / Hermaphrodite.

questions.text: Choose the correct larval-stage blend:
questions.explanation: Coracidium, procercoid, plerocercoid, cysticercus, cysticercoid, and hydatid forms are cestode-associated larval stages depending on the order. Miracidium belongs to trematodes, not cestodes, so it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Miracidium is a trematode larva, not a cestode larva.

questions.text: Choose the correct nematode oesophagus blend:
questions.explanation: Strongyloides is associated with rhabditiform larvae, making the Strongyloides/rhabditiform oesophagus pairing correct in this option set. Other pairings mismatch parasites with oesophageal morphology used for identification.
questions.keyConcept: Strongyloides larvae are classically rhabditiform in diagnostic stages.

questions.text: Regarding the life cycles of parasites which of the following is correct
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Heteroxenous parasites need more than one host in its life cycle. The item is testing a core parasitology definition, and the correct option fits the biologic meaning of the stem rather than merely sounding related. The distractors are adjacent concepts from other parasite groups, host categories, or transmission patterns.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield point: Regarding the life cycles of parasites which of the following is correct → Heteroxenous parasites need more than one host in its life cycle.
options: All obligatory parasites have direct life cycle

questions.text: Soil transmission of a parasitic infection is through
questions.explanation: Soil transmission commonly occurs when infective larvae actively penetrate skin, classically with hookworm larvae. Autoinfection refers to reinfection from the same host, while biological vectors transmit parasites through arthropod involvement rather than soil alone.
questions.keyConcept: Soil-transmitted helminths may infect by active skin penetration.

questions.text: Regarding Platyhelminths, choose the correct character
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Dorso-ventrally flattened. This item tests structural or life-cycle distinctions among platyhelminths, especially trematodes versus cestodes. The wrong options usually belong to another helminth group or a different developmental stage, so matching morphology to life cycle is the key.
questions.keyConcept: Platyhelminth morphology/life-cycle detail: Regarding Platyhelminths, choose the correct character → Dorso-ventrally flattened.

questions.text: The life cycle of all Nematodes is characterized by
questions.explanation: Nematodes pass through four larval stages before becoming adults. The infective stage is often the third-stage larva, but the universal life-cycle structure includes L1 through L4.
questions.keyConcept: Nematode life cycle has four larval stages.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer concerning the cyst stage of protozoa; it is
questions.explanation: The cyst is a resistant, inactive stage that survives unfavorable environmental conditions and often serves as the infective form. Trophozoites are active, motile, feeding forms and are usually less environmentally resistant.
questions.keyConcept: Protozoan cyst = resistant/infective dormant stage.

questions.text: Choose the correct character of Arthropods
questions.explanation: Arthropods are defined by segmented bodies, chitinous exoskeletons, and jointed appendages. The jointed appendages are the key feature reflected in the name Arthropoda.
questions.keyConcept: Arthropods are defined by jointed appendages, segmented bodies, and chitinous exoskeletons.

questions.text: In mechanical transmission of parasitic diseases in vector there is
questions.explanation: The correct answer is No multiplication and no development. The item is testing a core parasitology definition, and the correct option fits the biologic meaning of the stem rather than merely sounding related. The distractors are adjacent concepts from other parasite groups, host categories, or transmission patterns.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield point: In mechanical transmission of parasitic diseases in vector there is → No multiplication and no development.

questions.text: Advantage of direct diagnosis of parasitic diseases is
questions.explanation: Direct parasitologic diagnosis identifies the parasite or its stages directly, such as eggs, cysts, trophozoites, larvae, or blood forms. Its major advantage is that it usually requires no extra indirect testing and directly confirms the etiologic agent when positive.
questions.keyConcept: Direct diagnosis demonstrates the parasite/stage itself and can avoid extra tests.
options: Can differentiate between virulent and non-virulent strains

questions.text: One of the following agents is responsible for the immune mechanism against tissue helminths
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are central effector cells against tissue helminths because IgE-mediated responses recruit them and their granules can damage large parasites. Th1 macrophage responses are more important for intracellular microbes, while goblet and mast cells contribute to mucosal expulsion rather than direct tissue killing.
questions.keyConcept: Tissue helminths → Th2/IgE/eosinophil-mediated defense.

questions.text: A 37-year-old man presents with cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a small subapical focus of consolidation without cavitation, and histology shows epithelioid cells with giant cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Secondary pulmonary TB typically localizes to the apical/subapical lung and forms granulomas with epithelioid cells and giant cells. Primary TB more often forms a Ghon focus with lymph node involvement, while carcinoma and bilharziasis do not match the granulomatous apical TB picture.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary pulmonary TB favors apical/subapical lung with granulomatous inflammation.

questions.text: A 58-year-old woman with past chest troubles presents with severe back pain and X-ray destruction of vertebral bodies with deformity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pott disease is tuberculosis of the vertebral bodies, causing destruction, collapse and spinal deformity. The past chest history and vertebral destruction favor TB over metastatic carcinoma or leprosy.
questions.keyConcept: Pott disease = vertebral tuberculosis causing deformity.
options: Lung malignant tumor with bone metastasis

questions.text: A 60-year-old sandblaster develops progressive dyspnea without fever. Chest X-ray shows multiple upper-lung nodular opacities with a rounded nodule showing central caseation and restrictive lung disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Silicosis predisposes to tuberculosis, and the central caseation in an upper-lung nodule supports TB in a silica-exposed patient. Secondary TB can also affect upper lobes, but the occupational sandblasting history specifically points to TB predisposed by silicosis; carcinoma and pulmonary bilharziasis do not classically produce caseating granulomas in this pattern.
questions.keyConcept: Silicosis predisposes to pulmonary TB with upper-lobe caseating granulomas.

questions.text: A chronic inflammatory process shows macrophages transformed into epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, later central caseation necrosis, and finally fibrosis. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation: Caseating epithelioid granulomas are the classic tissue reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Leprosy and sarcoidosis may form granulomas but typically lack central caseation, and bilharziasis forms egg-centered granulomas rather than classic caseating tubercles.
questions.keyConcept: Caseating granuloma strongly suggests tuberculosis.

questions.text: A young man has swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck diagnosed as an abscess. Aspiration reveals cheesy material and leukocyte count is not elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cheesy material without leukocytosis suggests a tuberculous cold abscess due to caseation rather than an acute pyogenic abscess. The posterior cervical location fits tuberculous lymphadenitis/cold abscess.
questions.keyConcept: Cheesy cervical cold abscess suggests TB lymphadenitis.
options: Cervical Pott disease / TB with cold abscess

questions.text: A young patient has kyphosis and progressive lower-limb weakness. Lumbar X-ray shows vertebral destruction, and biopsy shows caseating granuloma. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Caseating granulomas in destroyed vertebrae with kyphosis are diagnostic of spinal TB (Pott disease). Metastasis and leprosy do not produce classic caseating granulomas in vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: Caseating vertebral granuloma with kyphosis = Pott disease.
options: Lung malignant tumor with bone metastasis

questions.text: Caseation necrosis in TB is mainly due to activation of:
questions.explanation: The source key attributes TB caseation necrosis mainly to cytotoxic cell-mediated injury. Th1 CD4 cells orchestrate macrophage activation, while epithelioid and Langhans giant cells are granuloma components rather than the main direct cytotoxic effector.
questions.keyConcept: TB caseation reflects cell-mediated immune injury within granulomas.

questions.text: Cold abscess is:
questions.explanation: A TB cold abscess represents caseous necrosis, commonly in lymph nodes, without the warmth and acute inflammatory signs of a pyogenic abscess. Liquefactive, fibrinoid and coagulative necrosis do not describe the typical tuberculous cold abscess.
questions.keyConcept: TB cold abscess = caseous necrosis without acute pyogenic signs.
options: An enlarged lymph node with liquefactive necrosis
An inflamed soft tissue with fibrinoid necrosis
An enlarged lymph node with coagulative necrosis
An enlarged lymph node with caseous necrosis

questions.text: Delayed hypersensitivity reaction in tuberculosis is beneficial because:
questions.explanation: Th1 delayed hypersensitivity activates macrophages, increasing their phagocytic and microbicidal capacity against tubercle bacilli. Caseation is a damaging consequence, not the beneficial effect, and the reaction does not directly prevent secondary infection.
questions.keyConcept: Benefit of TB delayed hypersensitivity: macrophage activation.
options: It increases the phagocytic power of macrophages

questions.text: Epithelioid cells are modified:
questions.explanation: Epithelioid cells are activated macrophages with abundant pink cytoplasm that aggregate in granulomas. They are not true epithelial cells despite their name.
questions.keyConcept: Epithelioid cells are activated macrophages.

questions.text: Fate of primary pulmonary TB depends on:
questions.explanation: The outcome of primary pulmonary TB depends on host resistance, organism virulence and infecting dose. These factors determine healing, progression or dissemination.
questions.keyConcept: TB outcome depends on host resistance, bacillary virulence and infecting dose.

questions.text: Features of the tuberculous reaction include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous granulomas contain epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis. Polymorphonuclear neutrophils are not a defining feature of the classic tuberculous granuloma.
questions.keyConcept: Classic TB granuloma = epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and caseation.

questions.text: Ghon focus consists of:
questions.explanation: The Ghon focus is a tuberculous granulomatous reaction in lung parenchyma. Syphilitic, bilharzial, nonspecific and foreign body reactions do not define a Ghon focus.
questions.keyConcept: Ghon focus is a tuberculous reaction in lung.

questions.text: Ghon focus occurs in the:
questions.explanation: A Ghon focus is the primary parenchymal lung lesion in primary pulmonary TB. Lymph node involvement is part of the Ghon complex, not the Ghon focus itself.
questions.keyConcept: Ghon focus = primary lung lesion of TB.

questions.text: Langhans giant cells result from fusion of:
questions.explanation: Langhans giant cells are multinucleated giant cells formed by fusion of epithelioid macrophages within granulomas. Their peripheral horseshoe nuclear arrangement is typical of tuberculous granulomas.
questions.keyConcept: Langhans giant cells form by fusion of epithelioid macrophages.

questions.text: Methods of infection in TB include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: TB infection occurs classically by inhalation, may occur by ingestion of infected milk, and can rarely be congenital/transplacental. Blood transfusion is not a typical route of TB transmission.
questions.keyConcept: TB spreads mainly by inhalation; ingestion and rare congenital spread occur, not blood transfusion.

questions.text: Mode of infection in primary pulmonary TB is:
questions.explanation: Primary pulmonary TB follows inhalation of aerosolized droplets containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Ingestion causes intestinal TB, and inoculation or transfusion are not typical pulmonary routes.
questions.keyConcept: Primary pulmonary TB is acquired by droplet inhalation.

questions.text: Mutation of which gene can be associated with TB infection susceptibility?
questions.explanation: NRAMP1 is involved in macrophage handling of intracellular pathogens and has been linked to susceptibility to mycobacterial infection. p53, BRCA-1 and C-myc are mainly cancer-related genes rather than TB susceptibility genes.
questions.keyConcept: NRAMP1 affects macrophage resistance to intracellular mycobacteria.

questions.text: Pathogenicity of tubercle bacilli is due to:
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis does not cause disease mainly by exotoxins, endotoxins or histiolytic enzymes. Tissue damage is largely immune-mediated through delayed type IV hypersensitivity and macrophage activation.
questions.keyConcept: TB pathology is driven by delayed type IV hypersensitivity.

questions.text: Primary TB of the intestine is more common in children because of:
questions.explanation: Primary intestinal TB in children is classically linked to ingestion of infected milk containing bovine tubercle bacilli. Low immunity may contribute, but the specific source mechanism is infected milk ingestion.
questions.keyConcept: Childhood primary intestinal TB is classically due to infected milk ingestion.

questions.text: Primary tuberculosis means:
questions.explanation: Primary TB is the first infection in a person not previously sensitized to tubercle bacilli. Immune and hypersensitivity reactions develop after infection, and the site is usually identifiable.
questions.keyConcept: Primary TB occurs in a previously uninfected host.
options: The host produces no immune reaction against tubercle bacilli
The patient is not previously infected by TB
The site of TB infection is not known
The tubercle bacilli produce no hypersensitivity reaction

questions.text: Sites of primary tuberculosis include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Primary TB occurs at entry sites such as lung, tonsil or intestine with regional lymph nodes. Kidney involvement is typically secondary/disseminated rather than a primary complex site.
questions.keyConcept: Primary TB sites: lung, intestine or tonsil with regional nodes; kidney is not typical primary site.

questions.text: TB cold abscess is a wrong name because:
questions.explanation: A TB cold abscess contains caseous material rather than true pus produced by acute pyogenic inflammation. It lacks the heat and acute inflammatory signs of an ordinary abscess.
questions.keyConcept: Cold abscess is “wrong” because it contains caseous material, not true pus.
options: It does not contain caseous material
It does not contain tubercle bacilli

questions.text: The edges of TB ulcers are:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous ulcers classically have undermined edges due to submucosal spread and tissue destruction. Everted edges suggest carcinoma rather than TB.
questions.keyConcept: TB ulcers characteristically have undermined edges.

questions.text: The ileocecal region is the commonest site of primary intestinal TB because:
questions.explanation: The ileocecal region contains abundant lymphoid tissue, which favors implantation and granulomatous response to ingested tubercle bacilli. Blood supply or a nonspecific weak area are not the main explanation.
questions.keyConcept: Ileocecal TB is common because the region is rich in lymphoid tissue.
options: It is rich in blood supply
It is rich in lymphoid tissue

questions.text: The immunologic activity of tubercle bacilli is due to:
questions.explanation: The protein part of the tubercle bacillus is responsible for antigenicity and immune reactivity. The lipid-rich wall contributes to resistance and virulence but is not the principal antigenic fraction in this source context.
questions.keyConcept: Tubercle bacillus protein fraction is antigenic.

questions.text: The lipid capsule of tubercle bacilli is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The lipid-rich mycobacterial wall helps bacilli resist destruction by lysosomal enzymes inside macrophages. Immunologic activity is mainly related to protein antigens, and multidrug resistance is not simply caused by the lipid capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Mycobacterial lipid-rich wall helps resist lysosomal destruction.

questions.text: The primary tuberculous complex consists of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A primary TB complex includes the primary focus at the site of infection, lymphangitis and regional lymphadenitis. A distant organ lesion indicates spread beyond the primary complex.
questions.keyConcept: Primary TB complex = focus + lymphangitis + regional lymphadenitis.
options: Tuberculosis of the site of infection

questions.text: Types of primary tuberculous complex include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is primary renal complex. Primary tuberculosis complexes occur at common entry sites such as lung, tonsillar/cervical, or intestinal locations; a primary renal complex is not a usual primary complex pattern. The duplicated cervical option was removed during final layout cleanup.
questions.keyConcept: Primary renal complex is not a usual form of primary tuberculosis complex.

questions.text: Which mediators are involved in the pathogenesis of TB?
questions.explanation: TB granuloma formation depends on IL-12-driven Th1 responses, interferon-gamma-mediated macrophage activation, and macrophage killing mechanisms including nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species. Therefore all listed mediators participate in TB pathogenesis.
questions.keyConcept: TB pathogenesis is Th1/macrophage driven: IL-12, IFN-gamma, NO and ROS.

questions.text: Which of the following is directly responsible for caseous necrosis?
questions.explanation: In TB, activated T cells release lymphokines/cytokines that drive macrophage activation and tissue necrosis within granulomas. Langhans giant cells and epithelioid cells are structural components of the granuloma, not the direct soluble mediators of caseation.
questions.keyConcept: Caseous necrosis in TB is mediated by lymphokine-driven cell-mediated immunity.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about secondary pulmonary TB?
questions.explanation: Secondary pulmonary TB occurs in a previously sensitized host and classically shows prominent caseation in the lung focus, often at the apex. Primary TB is first infection and more characteristically includes lymph node involvement as part of the primary complex.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary TB: apical lung lesion with extensive caseation.
options: It occurs due to infection by Mycobacterium TB for the first time
The lung focus shows extensive caseation
The lymph nodes show extensive caseation

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the structure of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: The protein fraction of the tubercle bacillus is chiefly responsible for antigenicity and hypersensitivity. TB pathogenesis is based on delayed type IV hypersensitivity, not type III; the lipid-rich wall helps resist destruction but does not provide motility.
questions.keyConcept: Tubercle bacillus proteins drive antigenicity; TB is type IV hypersensitivity.
options: It incites type III hypersensitivity reaction
The lipid capsule is responsible for its motility
The protein part is responsible for its antigenicity
The carbohydrate part is responsible for antigenicity

questions.text: Which type of pulmonary tuberculosis is most likely complicated by massive hemoptysis?
questions.explanation: Chronic fibrocaseous pulmonary TB can erode blood vessels in cavitary lesions, causing massive hemoptysis. Primary TB, miliary TB and tuberculous bronchopneumonia are less classically associated with massive bleeding from cavitation.
questions.keyConcept: Massive hemoptysis is a complication of chronic fibrocaseous/cavitary pulmonary TB.

questions.text: A 38-year-old patient has a hypopigmented anesthetic arm lesion; biopsy shows epithelioid non-caseating granuloma. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An anesthetic hypopigmented skin lesion with epithelioid granulomas indicates tuberculoid leprosy, which has strong cell-mediated immunity and few bacilli. Lepromatous leprosy shows lepra cells and many bacilli rather than well-formed epithelioid granulomas.
questions.keyConcept: Tuberculoid leprosy causes anesthetic hypopigmented lesions with epithelioid granulomas.

questions.text: A 56-year-old patient presents with facial disfiguring nodules and loss of eyelashes and eyebrows. Which statement is TRUE EXCEPT?
questions.explanation: This is lepromatous leprosy, in which lepra cells contain numerous bacilli because cell-mediated immunity is poor. The disease has low immunity, negative lepromin test and relatively less severe localized sensory loss than tuberculoid disease.
questions.keyConcept: Lepromatous leprosy: many bacilli in lepra cells, poor CMI, negative lepromin test.
options: It has an average incubation period of 3 years
It is associated with lowered immunity
Lepra cells show few lepra bacilli
It is usually associated with less severe sensory loss
It gives a negative lepromin test

questions.text: A large aggregate of epithelioid cells is diagnosed as:
questions.explanation: A granuloma is a focal aggregate of activated macrophages transformed into epithelioid cells, often with giant cells and lymphocytes. Granulation tissue is healing vascular connective tissue, and the other options are unrelated proliferative or cellular conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Granuloma = aggregate of epithelioid macrophages.

questions.text: A man with multiple sexual partners has a painless indurated penile ulcer with Treponema pallidum. Which microscopic finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Primary syphilitic chancre shows endarteritis/perivascular inflammation rich in plasma cells and lymphocytes. Gumma is a tertiary lesion, and suppurative/caseating granulomas or abscess formation do not match primary syphilis.
questions.keyConcept: Primary syphilis chancre shows perivascular plasma-cell-rich inflammation.

questions.text: A patient has airway obstruction, anosmia, speech difficulty, nasal bone/soft-tissue destruction and replacement by waxy nodular masses. Which pathological finding is the EXCEPTION?
questions.explanation: The presentation is rhinoscleroma, which shows Mikulicz cells, Russell bodies and histiocytic/plasma-cell-rich granulomatous inflammation. Lepra cells are foamy macrophages seen in lepromatous leprosy, not rhinoscleroma.
questions.keyConcept: Rhinoscleroma shows Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies; lepra cells belong to leprosy.

questions.text: All of the following are characteristic of chancre EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A primary syphilitic chancre is typically single, painless and indurated (hard), with regional non-suppurative lymphadenitis and spontaneous healing. Therefore “soft” is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Primary chancre is classically hard, painless and indurated.

questions.text: An 80-year-old man develops ataxia and paresis, then dies. Autopsy shows cerebral and ascending aortic atherosclerosis with aneurysm, a small scarred lobulated liver, and perivascular plasma cells with lymphocytes in organs. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tertiary syphilis can cause neurosyphilis, syphilitic aortitis with aneurysm, and gummatous scarring of organs such as the liver. Perivascular plasma-cell-rich inflammation supports syphilis rather than Alzheimer disease or amyloidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Tertiary syphilis causes neurosyphilis, aortitis/aneurysm and gummas.

questions.text: An adult has dry cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, recurrent eye inflammation/dryness, bilateral lung nodules, hilar lymphadenopathy, non-caseating granulomas, and skin nodules. Which finding is TRUE EXCEPT?
questions.explanation: This is sarcoidosis, which shows non-caseating granulomas with asteroid/Schaumann bodies, increased ACE and hypercalcemia. Russell bodies are plasma-cell immunoglobulin inclusions typical of rhinoscleroma/plasma-cell-rich inflammation, not sarcoidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Sarcoidosis: non-caseating granulomas, ACE elevation, hypercalcemia, asteroid/Schaumann bodies.
options: Giant cells contain asteroid and Schaumann bodies

questions.text: Concerning condyloma lata:
questions.explanation: Condyloma lata is a highly infectious mucocutaneous lesion of secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, not a viral lesion and not a tertiary feature. Since all listed statements are wrong, the correct choice is none of the above.
questions.keyConcept: Condyloma lata is an infectious secondary syphilis lesion.
options: The main feature of tertiary stage of syphilis

questions.text: Congenital syphilis may result in:
questions.explanation: Congenital syphilis can cause fetal loss, stillbirth, or live birth with syphilitic manifestations. Transplacental infection may affect fetal viability and multiple organs.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital syphilis can cause abortion, stillbirth or symptomatic live birth.

questions.text: Epithelioid granulomas are seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rhinoscleroma is characterized by Mikulicz cells and plasma cells with Russell bodies rather than typical epithelioid granulomas. Tuberculosis, leprosy and sarcoidosis are classic epithelioid granulomatous diseases, while toxoplasmosis may form granulomatous inflammatory lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Rhinoscleroma is dominated by Mikulicz cells, not classic epithelioid granulomas.

questions.text: Granulomas occur in all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: TB, sarcoidosis, leprosy and Crohn disease are granulomatous diseases. Amyloidosis is extracellular amyloid protein deposition, not a granulomatous inflammatory process.
questions.keyConcept: Amyloidosis is not a granulomatous disease.

questions.text: Inhalation is the mode of transmission in the following diseases EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a noninfectious granulomatous disease of unknown etiology, not transmitted by inhalation as an infection. TB, rhinoscleroma/laryngeoscleroma and leprosy can involve respiratory entry or droplets.
questions.keyConcept: Sarcoidosis is not an infectious inhalation-transmitted disease.

questions.text: Lepra cells are modified:
questions.explanation: Lepra cells are foamy macrophages packed with Mycobacterium leprae bacilli in lepromatous leprosy. They are modified histiocytes, not neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells or fibroblasts.
questions.keyConcept: Lepra cells are foamy macrophages in lepromatous leprosy.

questions.text: Mikulicz cells are modified:
questions.explanation: Mikulicz cells are large vacuolated histiocytes containing Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis in rhinoscleroma. Plasma cells may form Russell bodies, but the Mikulicz cell itself is histiocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Mikulicz cells are vacuolated histiocytes of rhinoscleroma.

questions.text: Modes of syphilitic infection include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Syphilis spreads mainly by sexual contact, transplacentally in congenital syphilis, and rarely through blood. Droplet infection is not a mode of syphilitic transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Syphilis spreads sexually and transplacentally, not by droplets.

questions.text: Most commonly, tertiary syphilis involves the:
questions.explanation: Tertiary syphilis most characteristically affects the cardiovascular system, especially the ascending aorta, causing syphilitic aortitis and aneurysm. Neurosyphilis is also important, but the commonest listed system is cardiovascular.
questions.keyConcept: Tertiary syphilis classically targets the cardiovascular system, especially the aorta.

questions.text: Russell bodies are modified:
questions.explanation: Russell bodies are eosinophilic immunoglobulin accumulations within plasma cells. They are common in plasma-cell-rich chronic inflammation such as rhinoscleroma.
questions.keyConcept: Russell bodies are immunoglobulin-filled plasma cells.

questions.text: Schaumann bodies could be characteristically seen within a lymph node with:
questions.explanation: Schaumann bodies are calcified/proteinaceous inclusions seen in giant cells of sarcoid-type non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas. Suppurative or caseating necrotizing granulomas fit infections such as mycetoma or TB rather than sarcoidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Schaumann bodies are characteristic of non-caseating sarcoid granulomas.

questions.text: The causative organism of syphilis can be demonstrated in the:
questions.explanation: Treponema pallidum can be demonstrated in lesions and around blood vessel walls, consistent with syphilitic endarteritis. Plasma cells are part of the inflammatory response but are not where the organism is classically demonstrated as an answer.
questions.keyConcept: Syphilitic organisms are demonstrated around vessel walls in syphilitic lesions.

questions.text: The commonest cardiovascular site affected by syphilis is the:
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular syphilis classically affects the ascending aorta, causing syphilitic aortitis and aneurysm. Small vessels and veins are not the usual commonest cardiovascular site.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiovascular syphilis targets the aorta.

questions.text: The following are all syphilitic lesions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Chancre, condyloma lata and gumma are lesions of syphilis. Condyloma acuminatum is a wart caused by HPV, not Treponema pallidum.
questions.keyConcept: Condyloma lata is syphilis; condyloma acuminata is HPV.

questions.text: Which disease is associated with peripheral neuropathy?
questions.explanation: Leprosy characteristically invades peripheral nerves, causing sensory loss, anesthesia and neuropathic deformities. Sarcoidosis, syphilis, rhinoscleroma and actinomycosis are not classically defined by peripheral nerve invasion in this module context.
questions.keyConcept: Leprosy causes peripheral neuropathy and anesthetic skin lesions.

questions.text: A 30-year-old farmer develops swollen foot with multiple skin sinuses discharging yellowish granules and areas of bone destruction. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Swollen foot with multiple sinuses, grains and bone destruction is classic Madura foot (mycetoma). Actinomycosis can form sulfur granules but usually involves cervicofacial or abdominal sites rather than the classic foot presentation.
questions.keyConcept: Madura foot/mycetoma presents with foot swelling, draining sinuses and grains.

questions.text: A 33-year-old farmer from Upper Egypt has a markedly edematous foot with multiple draining sinuses. Gram stain from a sinus shows gram-positive filamentous bacteria. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The swollen foot with draining sinuses and grains is mycetoma (Madura foot), and actinomycetoma may be caused by filamentous bacteria. Actinomycosis more classically affects cervicofacial tissues rather than presenting as Madura foot.
questions.keyConcept: Mycetoma/Madura foot presents with swollen foot, sinuses and grains.

questions.text: A patient has diffuse painless suppuration in the mandible/upper neck region with multiple sinuses discharging pus containing sulfur granules. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cervicofacial actinomycosis produces chronic suppurative granulomatous inflammation with draining sinuses and sulfur granules, often around the jaw. TB, gumma and sarcoidosis do not produce sulfur granules in this pattern.
questions.keyConcept: Cervicofacial actinomycosis causes jaw/neck sinuses with sulfur granules.

questions.text: Abdominal actinomycosis commonly affects the:
questions.explanation: Abdominal actinomycosis commonly affects the ileocecal region, often following mucosal injury or appendiceal disease. The other listed sites are less characteristic.
questions.keyConcept: Abdominal actinomycosis commonly involves the ileocecal region.

questions.text: Concerning Madura foot, it is:
questions.explanation: Madura foot (mycetoma) is a chronic suppurative granulomatous infection with swelling, sinuses and grains. It may be caused by fungi or filamentous bacteria, so it is not only fungal and is not an acute inflammation or gangrene.
questions.keyConcept: Madura foot is chronic suppurative granulomatous mycetoma.

questions.text: Which of the following is a suppurative granuloma?
questions.explanation: Mycetoma is a chronic suppurative granulomatous disease with sinuses and grains. Sarcoidosis is non-caseating, TB is caseating, leprosy is granulomatous/foamy depending on type, and rhinoscleroma is histiocytic with Mikulicz cells.
questions.keyConcept: Mycetoma is a suppurative granuloma.

questions.text: “Sulfur granules” are characteristically present in infection with:
questions.explanation: Actinomyces israelii causes suppurative granulomatous infection with draining sinuses containing yellow sulfur granules. Schistosoma causes egg granulomas, and the fungi listed do not classically produce sulfur granules.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfur granules in draining sinuses are classic for actinomycosis.

questions.text: A 40-year-old patient has progressive enlargement of the right leg for 6 years with thickening, fissures, inguinal lymphadenopathy and scrotal edema. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphedema, elephantiasis and scrotal edema are typical of lymphatic filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti. The other parasites cause hydatid disease, cutaneous leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis or trichinosis rather than elephantiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Wuchereria bancrofti causes lymphatic filariasis with elephantiasis and hydrocele.

questions.text: A 50-year-old man with urinary bilharziasis has hematuria and cystoscopy reveals a fungating bladder mass. All of the following are suspected in the pathology report EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Urinary bilharziasis predisposes to dysplasia and bladder carcinoma, especially squamous carcinoma but also urothelial and adenocarcinoma patterns. Basal cell carcinoma is a skin tumor and is not a suspected bladder pathology in this setting.
questions.keyConcept: Bilharziasis predisposes to bladder dysplasia/carcinoma, not basal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: All are features of portal hypertension EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Portal hypertension causes variceal bleeding with hematemesis/melena, splenic congestion with Gamna-Gandy bodies, and abdominal wall collaterals such as caput medusae. Hemoptysis is coughing blood from the respiratory tract and is not a portal hypertension feature.
questions.keyConcept: Portal hypertension causes hematemesis, melena, caput medusae and Gamna-Gandy bodies, not hemoptysis.

questions.text: All are pathological lesions of filariasis EXCEPT:
