questions.explanation: Filariasis causes lymphatic obstruction leading to lymphedema, elephantiasis, hydrocele and subcutaneous nodules. Splenomegaly is not a typical pathological lesion of lymphatic filariasis.
questions.keyConcept: Filariasis causes lymphatic obstruction: elephantiasis, hydrocele and lymphedema.

questions.text: All of the following may be causes of death in intestinal bilharziasis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Intestinal/hepatic schistosomiasis may cause portal hypertension with variceal bleeding, hepatic failure, hypersplenism and infection such as bronchopneumonia. Large-intestinal carcinoma is not the typical cause of death listed for intestinal bilharziasis.
questions.keyConcept: Intestinal bilharziasis deaths relate to portal hypertension/hepatic disease, not colon carcinoma.

questions.text: An Egyptian farmer has terminal hematuria. Cystoscopic biopsy reveals urinary bilharziasis with another lesion, leading the surgeon to remove the bladder. What is the other lesion?
questions.explanation: A carcinoma in a bladder affected by bilharziasis justifies cystectomy; the source key identifies transitional cell carcinoma. Sandy patches and ulcers are lesions of schistosomiasis but would not usually by themselves lead to bladder removal.
questions.keyConcept: Bladder carcinoma is the serious surgical lesion complicating urinary bilharziasis.

questions.text: Aspirate from a hydatid cyst consists of:
questions.explanation: Hydatid cyst fluid is typically clear serous fluid containing hydatid sand with scolices and hooklets. It is not mucin, pus, blood or caseous necrotic material.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatid cyst aspirate is clear serous fluid with hydatid sand.

questions.text: Brunn nests are due to:
questions.explanation: Brunn nests are invaginations/proliferations of urothelium into the lamina propria, representing hyperplasia. They are not by themselves dysplasia, metaplasia or neoplasia.
questions.keyConcept: Brunn nests are urothelial hyperplasia.

questions.text: Complications of filariasis include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Filariasis obstructs lymphatics causing lymphedema, elephantiasis, hydrocele and chyluria. Cystitis glandularis is a bladder mucosal metaplasia linked to chronic irritation such as urinary bilharziasis, not filariasis.
questions.keyConcept: Filariasis complications are lymphatic: elephantiasis, hydrocele, chyluria and lymphedema.

questions.text: Cystitis glandularis is due to:
questions.explanation: Cystitis glandularis is glandular metaplasia of the bladder mucosa, often related to chronic irritation. It differs from Brunn nests, which represent hyperplasia.
questions.keyConcept: Cystitis glandularis = glandular metaplasia of bladder mucosa.

questions.text: Gamna-Gandy nodules could be detected in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Gamna-Gandy bodies are siderotic fibrous nodules found in the spleen in portal hypertension and chronic congestion. Bilharzial periportal fibrosis causes portal hypertension, but the nodules themselves are detected in the spleen.
questions.keyConcept: Gamna-Gandy bodies are splenic siderotic nodules of portal hypertension.

questions.text: Renal failure in cases of urinary bilharziasis is due to:
questions.explanation: The printed key identifies bladder neck fibrosis as the cause of renal failure in urinary bilharziasis because it can obstruct urinary outflow and lead to back pressure. Brunn nests are mucosal hyperplasia, and unilateral obstruction alone is less likely to cause renal failure.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary bilharziasis can cause renal failure through obstructive fibrosis.

questions.text: Renal failure secondary to urinary bilharziasis is attributed to:
questions.explanation: Urinary bilharziasis can cause ureteric obstruction and back pressure, leading to bilateral hydronephrosis and renal failure. The other choices are not the usual mechanism of renal failure in urinary schistosomiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary bilharziasis causes renal failure through obstructive bilateral hydronephrosis.

questions.text: The cause of death in urinary bladder bilharziasis may be:
questions.explanation: Urinary bilharziasis may cause death by obstructive renal failure, bladder carcinoma, or cardiopulmonary complications in advanced disease. The source accepts all listed mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary bilharziasis death may result from renal failure, carcinoma or cardiac complications.

questions.text: The most dangerous complication of urinary bladder bilharziasis is:
questions.explanation: Bladder carcinoma is the most dangerous complication of chronic urinary schistosomiasis because of malignant progression. Renal failure is important, but the source key marks carcinoma as the most dangerous complication.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary bilharziasis most dangerous complication: bladder carcinoma.

questions.text: Urinary bladder bilharziasis can predispose to:
questions.explanation: Chronic urinary schistosomiasis causes epithelial injury, metaplasia and dysplasia that can predispose to bladder cancers, classically squamous carcinoma but also other carcinoma types in the source. Therefore all listed carcinoma types are accepted.
questions.keyConcept: Urinary bilharziasis predisposes to bladder carcinoma, especially squamous carcinoma.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Chemotherapy: Classification of Antibacterial Drugs, Inhibitors of Cell Wall Synthesis, Cephalosporins and Other B Lactams, Inhibitors of Protein Synthesis, Inhibitors of Nucleic Acids, Inhibitors of Folates, Clinical Aspects of Antimicrobials

questions.text: According to the WHO AWaRe classification, which antibiotic is NOT in the Reserve group?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is an Access-group antibiotic intended as first/second-line empirical therapy, not a last-resort Reserve agent. Imipenem, daptomycin and aztreonam are reserved for multidrug-resistant organisms.
questions.keyConcept: WHO AWaRe: amoxicillin = Access; carbapenems, daptomycin, aztreonam = Reserve.

questions.text: All of the following are effective in treatment of MRSA EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: MRSA is resistant to ordinary beta-lactams such as amoxicillin, while vancomycin, linezolid and daptomycin are accepted anti-MRSA options. Therefore amoxicillin is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: MRSA is treated with vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin, not amoxicillin.

questions.text: All the following antibacterial drugs may interfere with the plasma level of other drugs EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Ampicillin does not significantly affect hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes, so it does not alter other drug levels. Ciprofloxacin and chloramphenicol are enzyme inhibitors and rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin induces and ciprofloxacin/chloramphenicol inhibit CYP enzymes; ampicillin does not.

questions.text: All the following antibiotics are ototoxic EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Clindamycin is a lincosamide whose main hazard is pseudomembranous colitis, not ototoxicity. Aminoglycosides, vancomycin and high-dose macrolides can all impair hearing.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides, vancomycin and macrolides are ototoxic; clindamycin is not.

questions.text: All the following antibiotics should be avoided in pregnancy EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Azithromycin is a macrolide considered relatively safe in pregnancy, while tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides carry fetal risks (teeth/bone, cartilage, ototoxicity). Macrolides are the usual safe alternative for atypical infections in pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Avoid tetracyclines, quinolones, aminoglycosides in pregnancy; macrolides are safer.

questions.text: Large infrequent doses are superior to small frequent doses for all the following antibacterial drugs EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is time-dependent, so it relies on sustained levels rather than large peak doses, making it the exception. Daptomycin, amikacin and ciprofloxacin are concentration-dependent and benefit from large infrequent dosing.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin is time-dependent; daptomycin, aminoglycosides and quinolones are concentration-dependent.

questions.text: Nephrotoxic antibiotics do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is not characteristically nephrotoxic, whereas aminoglycosides, vancomycin and imipenem all carry renal toxicity risk. Penicillins may rarely cause interstitial nephritis but are not classed as directly nephrotoxic.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides, vancomycin and imipenem are nephrotoxic; amoxicillin is not.

questions.text: Regarding concentration-dependent antibiotics, which statement is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Concentration-dependent killers (aminoglycosides, quinolones, daptomycin) work best as large, infrequent doses that drive peak levels far above the MIC, so the statement favoring small frequent doses is wrong. Small frequent dosing is the principle for time-dependent agents instead.
questions.keyConcept: Concentration-dependent antibiotics: large infrequent doses, peak >>MIC (aminoglycosides, quinolones, daptomycin).
options: Large infrequent doses are superior to small frequent doses
Bactericidal effect is increased at higher drug concentration
Optimum effect is achieved at concentrations about 10 times the MIC
Small frequent doses are superior to large infrequent doses

questions.text: Regarding time-dependent antibiotics, which statement is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Time-dependent agents (beta-lactams, vancomycin) depend on the time their level stays above MIC, so small frequent doses (or infusions) are superior, making the claim that large infrequent doses are better wrong. Raising the concentration well above MIC does not add killing for these drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Time-dependent antibiotics: efficacy depends on T>MIC, favor small frequent doses (beta-lactams, vancomycin).
options: Bactericidal effect is not increased at higher drug concentration
Large infrequent doses are superior to small frequent doses
Optimum effect is achieved at concentration above 2-4 times the MIC
Small frequent doses are superior to large infrequent doses

questions.text: The following antibacterial drug is NOT a cell wall synthesis inhibitor:
questions.explanation: Clindamycin inhibits protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit, not the cell wall. Imipenem, piperacillin (beta-lactams) and vancomycin all target cell wall synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin and beta-lactams inhibit cell wall synthesis; clindamycin inhibits the 50S ribosome.

questions.text: The following antibiotic is NOT a protein synthesis inhibitor:
questions.explanation: Meropenem is a carbapenem beta-lactam that inhibits cell wall synthesis, not protein synthesis. Tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, streptogramins and linezolid all act on the bacterial ribosome.
questions.keyConcept: Carbapenems inhibit cell wall synthesis; ribosomal inhibitors include tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, streptogramins, linezolid.

questions.text: The following antibiotic is not a Reserve group drug according to WHO AWaRe classification:
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin belongs to the Access group rather than the Reserve group. Carbapenems and resistant-organism agents such as daptomycin are Reserve in this teaching context, while aztreonam is treated as higher-restriction than amoxicillin.
questions.keyConcept: Amoxicillin is Access, not Reserve, in WHO AWaRe classification.

questions.text: The following drug is incorrectly matched to its mechanism of action:
questions.explanation: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and causes misreading of mRNA, not a 50S inhibitor. The other mechanism pairings are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides bind 30S; macrolides/clindamycin/chloramphenicol/linezolid bind 50S.

questions.text: The following drug is not excreted through bile:
questions.explanation: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside and is eliminated mainly by the kidney, not by biliary excretion. Azithromycin, doxycycline, cefoperazone and rifampicin have important biliary elimination.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are renally excreted, not biliary.

questions.text: The following drugs increase the risk of bleeding if taken with warfarin EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin does not meaningfully potentiate warfarin, while streptogramins (enzyme inhibition), cefoperazone (hypoprothrombinemia) and sulfonamides (protein-binding displacement) all raise bleeding risk. This makes amoxicillin the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoperazone, sulfonamides and streptogramins potentiate warfarin; amoxicillin does not.

questions.text: The following is NOT an indication for antimicrobial drug combination:
questions.explanation: Combination therapy generally increases cost rather than decreasing it, so reducing cost is not a valid indication. The legitimate reasons include limiting resistance, lowering toxicity, covering polymicrobial infections, and broad empirical cover.
questions.keyConcept: Drug combinations are used to limit resistance, reduce toxicity, and broaden cover - not to cut cost.
options: To provide broad-spectrum empirical therapy in severely ill patients

questions.text: Which drug does NOT increase bleeding risk when taken with warfarin?
questions.explanation: Streptogramins and sulfonamides can inhibit metabolism or displace warfarin, and cefoperazone can cause hypoprothrombinemia, increasing bleeding. Amoxicillin is the exception in this source-keyed set.
questions.keyConcept: Warfarin bleeding risk rises with sulfonamides, streptogramins and cefoperazone; amoxicillin is the exception here.

questions.text: Which drug is NOT matched with its adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline is not a hepatic enzyme inducer; rifampicin is the classic enzyme inducer. The other adverse-effect pairings are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin, not doxycycline, is the classic enzyme inducer.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a concentration-dependent antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Erythromycin is a macrolide and acts as a time-dependent, largely bacteriostatic agent, not a concentration-dependent one. Gentamycin and the fluoroquinolones are classic concentration-dependent killers.
questions.keyConcept: Macrolides are time-dependent; aminoglycosides and quinolones are concentration-dependent.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a semisynthetic penicillin?
questions.explanation: Penicillin G is a natural penicillin produced directly by Penicillium, not a semisynthetic derivative. Ampicillin, cloxacillin and carbenicillin are all semisynthetic modifications of the penicillin nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin G is natural; ampicillin/cloxacillin/carbenicillin are semisynthetic.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a time-dependent antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Quinolones are concentration-dependent, so they are the exception among these time-dependent agents. Penicillins, cephalosporins and vancomycin all rely on time above MIC.
questions.keyConcept: Quinolones = concentration-dependent; beta-lactams and vancomycin = time-dependent.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic principles is WRONG?
questions.explanation: The post-antibiotic effect is defined as continued suppression of bacterial growth AFTER drug levels fall below the MIC, so describing it as occurring while levels are still above MIC is wrong. Beta-lactams show little PAE, while aminoglycosides and daptomycin are concentration-dependent with a marked PAE.
questions.keyConcept: Post-antibiotic effect = growth suppression persisting after the level drops below MIC.
options: Bacterial regrowth starts soon after the trough falls below the MIC for beta-lactam antibiotics
Aminoglycosides are more effective given as a single daily dose than every 8 hours
Post-antibiotic effect is the persistence of antibacterial effect while the drug level is still above the MIC
Daptomycin is concentration-dependent with a post-antibiotic effect

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin causes pseudomembranous colitis and is not an indication for its treatment, so this statement is wrong. Linezolid's MAO inhibition and rifampicin/ciprofloxacin enzyme effects are correct; chloramphenicol's serious marrow toxicity is the key concern.
questions.keyConcept: Clindamycin causes, not treats, pseudomembranous colitis.
options: Linezolid has MAO-inhibiting action and may increase sympathomimetic effects
Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer while ciprofloxacin is an enzyme inhibitor
Pseudomembranous colitis is an indication for clindamycin
Agranulocytosis is the most serious adverse effect of chloramphenicol

questions.text: Match each antimicrobial class with its mechanism of action.
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams and vancomycin inhibit different steps in cell-wall synthesis. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on 30S ribosomes, chloramphenicol and macrolides act on 50S ribosomes, quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase, and rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanism map: cell wall inhibitors, 30S/50S protein synthesis inhibitors, quinolones, and rifampicin.

pairs.target: Inhibits early peptidoglycan synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala
Cause mRNA misreading on 30S ribosome and require oxygen-dependent uptake
Block aminoacyl-tRNA access to the 30S ribosomal subunit
Inhibits peptidyl transferase on the 50S ribosomal subunit

questions.text: Match each antimicrobial combination with its correct partner.
questions.explanation: Augmentin contains amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, while Unasyn contains ampicillin plus sulbactam. Brucellosis is treated with doxycycline plus rifampicin, and co-trimoxazole combines a sulfonamide with trimethoprim for sequential folate blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Know fixed antimicrobial combinations: Augmentin, Unasyn, co-trimoxazole, and brucellosis therapy.

questions.text: Match each antimicrobial with its characteristic side effect.
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin and can cause kernicterus in neonates. Chloramphenicol causes gray baby syndrome, outdated tetracycline causes Fanconi-like renal tubular dysfunction, and rapid vancomycin infusion causes red man syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Classic toxicity matching: sulfonamides-kernicterus, chloramphenicol-gray baby, outdated tetracycline-Fanconi, vancomycin-red man.

questions.text: Match each drug with its possible drug interaction.
questions.explanation: Cilastatin protects imipenem from renal metabolism, and probenecid blocks renal secretion of penicillin. Daptomycin adds statin myopathy risk, rifampicin induces enzymes, streptogramins inhibit hepatic metabolism, sulfonamides displace protein-bound drugs, linezolid has MAO-inhibitor interactions, and quinolones chelate antacids.
questions.keyConcept: High-yield interactions: cilastatin-imipenem, probenecid-penicillin, daptomycin-statins, rifampicin-induction, linezolid-SSRI, quinolones-antacids.

pairs.target: Increases risk of myopathy with statins
Decreases plasma levels of drugs by enzyme induction

questions.text: A man with multiple antibiotic resistance is given a prophylactic IV dose of antibiotic before surgery. As it is being infused he becomes flushed over most of his body. Which antibiotic is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Rapid IV infusion of vancomycin causes non-immunological histamine release producing flushing of the upper body, the classic red man syndrome. It is an infusion-rate reaction rather than a true allergy, and slowing the infusion with antihistamine support reduces the reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Rapid IV vancomycin causes red man syndrome (histamine-mediated flushing).

questions.text: All the following are true about penicillins EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Penicillins and aminoglycosides must never be mixed in the same syringe/bolus because they chemically inactivate each other, so this statement is false. Penicillins are pregnancy-safe, cross inflamed meninges, and are prolonged by probenecid.
questions.keyConcept: Never mix penicillins and aminoglycosides in one syringe - they inactivate each other.
options: Safe in pregnancy despite crossing the placenta
Can cross the BBB in meningitis
Concomitant administration of probenecid can prolong their action
Injected with an aminoglycoside as one single IV bolus in bacterial endocarditis

questions.text: All the following drugs are sensitive to beta-lactamase enzyme EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Oxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin whose side chain shields the beta-lactam ring from the enzyme. Amoxicillin, penicillin G and benzathine penicillin are all hydrolysed by beta-lactamase.
questions.keyConcept: Oxacillin (anti-staph penicillin) resists beta-lactamase; natural/amino-penicillins do not.

questions.text: As regards amoxicillin, the following statement is WRONG:
questions.explanation: Because amoxicillin is almost completely absorbed in the upper gut, little reaches the colon, so it is NOT preferred for shigella dysentery (ampicillin, which is less absorbed, is favored). Its complete absorption, lower diarrhea risk and beta-lactamase sensitivity are all true.
questions.keyConcept: Amoxicillin's complete absorption makes ampicillin better for intraluminal shigellosis.
options: It has less incidence of diarrhea and higher serum level than ampicillin
It is preferred to ampicillin in shigella dysentery
It is a broad-spectrum penicillin susceptible to beta-lactamase enzyme

questions.text: Clavulanic acid is combined with amoxicillin because:
questions.explanation: Clavulanic acid is a suicide inhibitor of beta-lactamase, protecting amoxicillin from enzymatic breakdown so it can act on beta-lactamase-producing organisms. It has negligible intrinsic antibacterial activity of its own.
questions.keyConcept: Clavulanic acid is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects amoxicillin.
options: It kills bacteria not killed by amoxicillin
It attenuates the allergic reaction to amoxicillin
It counteracts the adverse effects of amoxicillin
It inhibits the beta-lactamases that would destroy amoxicillin
It retards the renal excretion of amoxicillin

questions.text: Compared with other penicillins, piperacillin poses a greater risk of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Antipseudomonal penicillins such as piperacillin interfere with platelet function and can prolong bleeding time, raising bleeding risk. This is distinct from the renal, CNS or GI effects listed.
questions.keyConcept: Antipseudomonal penicillins (piperacillin) impair platelets and increase bleeding risk.

questions.text: Concomitant therapy of probenecid with penicillin leads to:
questions.explanation: Probenecid inhibits renal tubular secretion of penicillin, thereby increasing and prolonging penicillin plasma levels. It is not used to reduce penicillin levels or primarily alter probenecid levels in this context.
questions.keyConcept: Probenecid increases penicillin levels by blocking renal tubular secretion.

questions.text: In the previous case (flushing during IV antibiotic infusion), this adverse effect can be avoided by:
questions.explanation: Because red man syndrome is histamine-mediated and infusion-rate dependent, it is prevented by slowing the infusion and pretreating with an antihistamine. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed and would not treat a systemic infection.
questions.keyConcept: Prevent red man syndrome by slow infusion and antihistamine premedication.
options: Pretreating the patient with an antihistamine and slowing the infusion
Giving the drug combined with aminoglycosides

questions.text: Select the antibiotic whose dose must be reduced in patients with renal insufficiency:
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is almost entirely cleared by the kidney and is nephrotoxic, so its dose must be reduced and levels monitored in renal insufficiency. Oxacillin and cefoperazone are eliminated largely in bile, and ampicillin has a wide safety margin.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin is renally cleared - reduce dose and monitor levels in renal impairment.

questions.text: The addition of all the following prolongs duration of action of penicillin EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Benzathine and procaine form depot penicillin preparations, and probenecid reduces renal tubular secretion of penicillin, all prolonging action. Clavulanic acid inhibits beta-lactamase and broadens spectrum, but does not prolong duration.
questions.keyConcept: Benzathine/procaine/probenecid prolong penicillin action; clavulanate broadens spectrum.

questions.text: The drug of choice in patients allergic to penicillin is:
questions.explanation: Erythromycin is a macrolide and is classically used as an alternative in patients allergic to penicillin, especially for susceptible respiratory and gram-positive infections. Imipenem, meropenem and cefazolin are beta-lactams and may be unsuitable in significant beta-lactam allergy.
questions.keyConcept: Macrolides such as erythromycin are classic alternatives in penicillin allergy.

questions.text: The following antibiotics are highly hydrophilic and not used orally for systemic effect:
questions.explanation: Vancomycin and neomycin are highly polar and are not absorbed orally for systemic effect; oral use is for local gastrointestinal action. Clindamycin is orally absorbed and can be used systemically.
questions.keyConcept: Oral vancomycin and neomycin act locally in the gut because they are poorly absorbed.

questions.text: The following is NOT an adverse effect of vancomycin:
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is a TREATMENT for pseudomembranous colitis, not a cause, so this is the exception. Its recognized toxicities are nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, red man syndrome and infusion-related fever/rigors.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin treats C. difficile colitis; it does not cause it.

questions.text: The following is a WRONG statement about the pharmacokinetics of penicillins:
questions.explanation: Penicillins penetrate the CSF only when the meninges are inflamed, so the dose must be kept HIGH (not reduced) while treating meningitis as penetration falls when inflammation resolves. The other statements about absorption, placental safety and renal excretion are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin CSF entry needs inflamed meninges; maintain high meningitis doses.
options: Amoxicillin is completely absorbed with less risk of diarrhea than ampicillin
They cross the placenta during pregnancy and are not teratogenic
They cross the BBB during inflammation, so the dose should be reduced after the inflammation improves
They are excreted mainly renally by filtration and active secretion

questions.text: The following is an INCORRECT statement about penicillin combinations:
questions.explanation: In penicillin-aminoglycoside synergy the cell-wall-active penicillin enhances entry of the AMINOGLYCOSIDE into the organism, not the other way round, so this statement is reversed and incorrect. The other combinations are correctly described.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin damages the wall so the aminoglycoside can enter - synergy aids aminoglycoside uptake.
options: Combining procaine and benzathine with penicillin G prolongs its action
Combining amoxicillin with clavulanic acid broadens its spectrum against beta-lactamase producers
Combining penicillins with aminoglycosides increases the penicillin uptake by the organism
Combining penicillins with probenecid decreases their renal excretion

questions.text: The following is given in combination with ampicillin to broaden its spectrum against beta-lactamase producers:
questions.explanation: Sulbactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor combined with ampicillin (as Unasyn) to protect it from enzymatic destruction. Benzathine/procaine only prolong action and probenecid only blocks renal secretion.
questions.keyConcept: Ampicillin + sulbactam (Unasyn) overcomes beta-lactamase.

questions.text: The following penicillin is effective against Pseudomonas infections:
questions.explanation: Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Ampicillin lacks antipseudomonal activity and the cephalosporins listed are not antipseudomonal agents.
questions.keyConcept: Antipseudomonal penicillins = piperacillin, ticarcillin, carbenicillin.

questions.text: The following penicillin preparation is NOT suitable for the oral route:
questions.explanation: Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin that is acid-labile and must be given parenterally. Amoxicillin, ampicillin and oxacillin are acid-stable and can be taken orally.
questions.keyConcept: Piperacillin is parenteral (acid-unstable antipseudomonal penicillin).

questions.text: The penicillin G preparation with the longest duration of action is:
questions.explanation: Benzathine penicillin is a depot preparation released very slowly from the IM site, giving the longest duration (weeks), which is why it is used for rheumatic fever prophylaxis and syphilis. Sodium/potassium salts are short-acting and procaine penicillin is intermediate.
questions.keyConcept: Benzathine penicillin = longest-acting depot form (rheumatic fever prophylaxis, syphilis).

questions.text: Which feature is NOT shared by vancomycin and aminoglycosides?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent with a post-antibiotic effect, but vancomycin is classically time-dependent, so this is not shared. Both are poorly absorbed orally, can cause ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity, and can be used orally for local gut effects in specific settings.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent; vancomycin is time-dependent.
options: Taken orally for local effect in the GIT

questions.text: Which of the following drugs is penicillinase-resistant and given orally?
questions.explanation: Augmentin (amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) is taken orally and resists penicillinase because clavulanic acid inhibits the beta-lactamase enzyme. Ampicillin, amoxicillin and penicillin V are all destroyed by penicillinase.
questions.keyConcept: Clavulanic acid (in Augmentin) protects amoxicillin from penicillinase and is given orally.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are excreted renally?
questions.explanation: Penicillin, vancomycin and cefazolin are all eliminated primarily by the kidney, so all of them require dose adjustment in renal impairment. This contrasts with biliary-excreted agents such as cefoperazone and ceftriaxone.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin, vancomycin and cefazolin are renally excreted (adjust in renal failure).

questions.text: Which penicillin preparation is antipseudomonal and acid unstable?
questions.explanation: Carbenicillin is an antipseudomonal carboxypenicillin that is acid unstable and therefore not a standard oral penicillin. Oxacillin is beta-lactamase resistant and penicillin G is natural parenteral penicillin.
questions.keyConcept: Carbenicillin/ticarcillin are acid-unstable antipseudomonal penicillins.

questions.text: Which penicillin preparation resists beta-lactamase-producing organisms?
questions.explanation: Oxacillin belongs to the penicillinase-resistant (anti-staphylococcal) penicillins and is stable against beta-lactamase. The natural and amino-penicillins listed are readily destroyed by the enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: Oxacillin, nafcillin, and cloxacillin resist staphylococcal beta-lactamase enzymes.

questions.text: Match each penicillin or related beta-lactam with its characteristic feature.
questions.explanation: Penicillin G is natural and parenteral, oxacillin resists beta-lactamase, ampicillin and amoxicillin are aminopenicillins, benzathine penicillin is depot long-acting, piperacillin is antipseudomonal with bleeding risk, and cefoxitin is a second-generation cephalosporin with anaerobic coverage. This preserves the original matching relationship while using the updated ASU matching schema.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-lactam feature matching distinguishes natural, antistaphylococcal, aminopenicillin, depot, antipseudomonal, and cephamycin agents.

pairs.target: Broad-spectrum penicillin with less diarrhea than ampicillin
Very long half-life; used for rheumatic fever prophylaxis

questions.text: Match each resistant-organism drug with its characteristic feature.
questions.explanation: Daptomycin is a concentration-dependent lipopeptide used for resistant non-pulmonary gram-positive infection. Ceftaroline is the anti-MRSA fifth-generation cephalosporin, ticarcillin is an acid-unstable antipseudomonal penicillin, cefepime is fourth generation, and linezolid is active orally and IV against resistant gram-positive organisms.
questions.keyConcept: Resistant-organism drug features: daptomycin membrane, ceftaroline anti-MRSA, ticarcillin antipseudomonal, cefepime 4th gen, linezolid oral/IV VRE.

pairs.target: Concentration-dependent drug used for non-pneumonic VRSA/VRE infection
Fifth-generation cephalosporin effective against MRSA/VRSA in the source set
Effective against vancomycin-resistant strains and available orally and IV

questions.text: A 36-year-old female with leukemia has fever. Her blood smear reveals gram-negative bacilli and she has a history of penicillin allergy. Which of the following is best for her?
questions.explanation: Aztreonam covers aerobic gram-negative bacilli and has no cross-reactivity with penicillins, making it ideal in a penicillin-allergic patient with gram-negative sepsis. Imipenem and cefazolin carry cross-allergy risk and erythromycin lacks gram-negative bacillary cover.
questions.keyConcept: Aztreonam is the safe gram-negative beta-lactam in penicillin allergy.

questions.text: A patient allergic to penicillin with renal impairment has mixed gram-negative aerobic bacilli and beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae infection. The best choice is:
questions.explanation: Aztreonam covers aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including beta-lactamase producers), is beta-lactamase stable and is safe in penicillin allergy. Cephalosporins risk cross-allergy and vancomycin has no gram-negative activity.
questions.keyConcept: Aztreonam: gram-negative cover that is safe in penicillin allergy.

questions.text: Cefoperazone is associated with a high risk of:
questions.explanation: Cefoperazone has an N-methylthiotetrazole side chain that causes hypoprothrombinemia and a disulfiram-like reaction, increasing bleeding especially with warfarin. This is its hallmark adverse effect.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoperazone (NMTT side chain) causes hypoprothrombinemia/bleeding and alcohol intolerance.
options: Bleeding tendencies in patients taking warfarin
Severe allergic reactions in patients with mild penicillin allergy

questions.text: Regarding aztreonam, which of the following is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Aztreonam is a monobactam with a NARROW spectrum limited to aerobic gram-negative bacilli, so calling it the broadest-spectrum beta-lactam is wrong (that description fits the carbapenems). It is safe in penicillin allergy and is beta-lactamase stable.
questions.keyConcept: Aztreonam = narrow aerobic gram-negative cover, safe in penicillin allergy.
options: Effective mainly against aerobic gram-negative organisms
Can be used in patients allergic to penicillins

questions.text: Regarding imipenem, which of the following is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Imipenem is proconvulsant and is AVOIDED in meningitis, where meropenem is preferred, so this statement is incorrect. Imipenem is the broadest-spectrum beta-lactam, is given with cilastatin to block renal dehydropeptidase, and resists most beta-lactamases.
questions.keyConcept: Use meropenem (not imipenem) in meningitis; imipenem lowers seizure threshold.
options: Preferred to meropenem in patients with meningitis and penicillin allergy
Cilastatin can guard against its renal toxic metabolites

questions.text: The following is WRONG as regards cephalosporins:
questions.explanation: Bleeding and a disulfiram-like alcohol reaction are linked to the NMTT side chain of CEFOPERAZONE, not ceftriaxone, so this statement is wrong. Cefoperazone is biliary and CNS-poor, while ceftriaxone is biliary and useful in typhoid/gonorrhea.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoperazone (not ceftriaxone) causes hypoprothrombinemia and alcohol intolerance.
options: Cefoperazone is 3rd generation and cannot cross the BBB
Ceftriaxone is long-acting and used in typhoid fever and gonorrhea
Both cefoperazone and ceftriaxone are secreted in bile
Bleeding and alcohol intolerance are more common with ceftriaxone

questions.text: Which cephalosporin has increased activity against anaerobic bacteria such as Bacteroides fragilis (e.g. in peritonitis)?
questions.explanation: Cefoxitin is a cephamycin with notable activity against anaerobes including Bacteroides fragilis, useful in mixed intra-abdominal infection. The other cephalosporins listed lack reliable anaerobic cover.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoxitin (cephamycin) is the anti-anaerobe cephalosporin.

questions.text: Which cephalosporin preparations are highly concentrated in bone?
questions.explanation: Both cefazolin (used in orthopedic surgical prophylaxis) and ceftriaxone are highly concentrated in bone, so the answer is 'A and D'. This bone penetration underlies their use in bone-related infection and prophylaxis.
questions.keyConcept: Cefazolin and ceftriaxone achieve high bone concentrations.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cell wall inhibitor useful against anaerobes?
questions.explanation: Both cefoxitin (a cephamycin) and imipenem (a carbapenem) are beta-lactam cell wall inhibitors with useful anaerobic activity, so the answer is 'B or D'. Clindamycin also covers anaerobes but inhibits protein synthesis, and aztreonam covers only aerobic gram-negatives.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoxitin and imipenem are anti-anaerobe beta-lactams; aztreonam covers only aerobic gram-negatives.

questions.text: Which of the following is the best drug for biliary infection?
questions.explanation: Cefoperazone is a third-generation cephalosporin excreted mainly in bile, achieving high biliary concentrations ideal for biliary tract infection. The other agents are excreted renally and reach lower biliary levels.
questions.keyConcept: Cefoperazone and ceftriaxone are biliary-excreted - best for biliary infection.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about cephalosporins?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone is biliary-excreted and long-acting, making it effective in biliary tract infection and typhoid fever. Cefazolin (not cephalexin) is preferred for surgical prophylaxis, cefoxitin does cover anaerobes, and cefoperazone is sensitive to beta-lactamase.
questions.keyConcept: Ceftriaxone is used in biliary infection and typhoid (biliary excretion, long t1/2).
options: Cephalexin is preferred to cefazolin in surgical prophylaxis
Cefoxitin is not used in anaerobic infections
Ceftriaxone can be used in biliary tract infection and typhoid fever

questions.text: Match each cephalosporin antibiotic with its most appropriate use.
questions.explanation: Cefazolin is used for surgical and orthopedic prophylaxis, cefoxitin is useful for mixed anaerobic infection, ceftriaxone crosses inflamed meninges and is biliary-excreted, and cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin used for resistant organisms and meningitis coverage. This preserves the original matching relationship while using the updated ASU matching schema.
questions.keyConcept: Cephalosporin use map: cefazolin-prophylaxis, cefoxitin-anaerobes, ceftriaxone-meningitis/biliary, cefepime-resistant meningitis coverage.

questions.text: Match each cephalosporin with its most appropriate use in the alternate source set.
questions.explanation: Cefazolin is the surgical prophylaxis agent, cefoxitin covers mixed anaerobic infections, ceftriaxone is useful for meningitis and biliary infection, and cefuroxime is matched to community-acquired pneumonia in the alternate source set. This preserves the original matching relationship while using the updated ASU matching schema.
questions.keyConcept: Alternate cephalosporin map includes cefuroxime for community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.text: A bacteriostatic protein synthesis inhibitor that is the drug of choice for atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia) is:
questions.explanation: Macrolides such as azithromycin concentrate intracellularly and are first-line for atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma, Legionella and Chlamydia. Aminoglycosides and cell wall agents are ineffective against these wall-deficient/intracellular organisms.
questions.keyConcept: Macrolides are drug of choice for atypical (Mycoplasma/Legionella/Chlamydia) pneumonia.

questions.text: A patient on antibacterial therapy is going to have an operation in which a skeletal muscle relaxant may be used. Which antimicrobial increases the risk of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides can cause neuromuscular blockade by inhibiting acetylcholine release and reducing postsynaptic sensitivity. This effect can be dangerous when combined with skeletal muscle relaxants during anesthesia; the other options do not classically produce this interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides potentiate neuromuscular blockade, especially with muscle relaxants.

questions.text: A patient with myasthenia gravis is at greatest risk of worsening muscle weakness if given which antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin block presynaptic acetylcholine release and reduce postsynaptic sensitivity, producing neuromuscular blockade that is especially dangerous in myasthenia gravis. The other agents do not impair neuromuscular transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides cause neuromuscular blockade - avoid in myasthenia gravis.

questions.text: A primarily bacteriostatic antibiotic that becomes bactericidal at high concentrations is:
questions.explanation: Macrolides such as erythromycin are primarily bacteriostatic but may become bactericidal at high concentrations against susceptible organisms. Tetracyclines remain bacteriostatic, while ampicillin is primarily bactericidal as a cell wall inhibitor.
questions.keyConcept: Erythromycin is usually bacteriostatic but can be cidal at high concentrations.

questions.text: Absorption of oral tetracyclines is decreased by:
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines form insoluble chelates with divalent and trivalent cations, so milk (calcium), antacids (aluminum/magnesium) and iron salts markedly reduce their absorption. They should be taken apart from these products.
questions.keyConcept: Di/trivalent cations (milk, antacids, iron) chelate tetracyclines and block absorption.

questions.text: All the following drugs are used in vancomycin-resistant enterococci EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Linezolid, daptomycin and streptogramins can be used for resistant gram-positive infections including VRE in source teaching. Gentamicin alone is not a treatment for vancomycin-resistant enterococci.
questions.keyConcept: VRE options include linezolid, daptomycin and streptogramins; not gentamicin alone.

questions.text: Aminoglycosides are bactericidal and exhibit:
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent bactericidal activity and a prolonged post-antibiotic effect, which is why once-daily high-dose regimens are effective and reduce toxicity. They are not absorbed orally and require aerobic conditions for uptake.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides = concentration-dependent killing + long post-antibiotic effect (once-daily dosing).
options: Time-dependent killing with no post-antibiotic effect
Concentration-dependent killing with a significant post-antibiotic effect

questions.text: Aplastic anemia and optic neuritis are adverse effects of:
questions.explanation: The source key assigns this adverse-effect pair to chloramphenicol, whose major serious toxicity is aplastic anemia; optic neuritis is also classically listed in some teaching sources. Daptomycin causes myopathy, ciprofloxacin causes tendinopathy/QT effects, and gentamicin causes ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol is classically associated with aplastic anemia; daptomycin with myopathy.

questions.text: Concerning clindamycin, which statement is TRUE?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin has excellent activity against many anaerobes and gram-positive organisms. It can cause pseudomembranous colitis rather than treat it, lacks strong aerobic gram-negative coverage and is not a beta-lactamase inhibitor.
questions.keyConcept: Clindamycin covers anaerobes but classically causes C. difficile colitis.
options: It is effective against anaerobic infections
It is the treatment of choice for pseudomembranous colitis
It has strong gram-negative aerobic coverage

questions.text: Daptomycin is best described as:
questions.explanation: Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide that disrupts the gram-positive cell membrane, given parenterally for MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci. It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant so cannot be used for pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: Daptomycin = parenteral bactericidal lipopeptide for resistant gram-positives (not for pneumonia).
options: An oral agent for gram-negative infection
A bactericidal lipopeptide used IM/IV for resistant gram-positive organisms

questions.text: Gray baby syndrome in neonates is caused by:
questions.explanation: Neonates lack mature hepatic glucuronyl transferase and renal excretion, so chloramphenicol accumulates and causes gray baby syndrome (cyanosis, hypotension, vasomotor collapse). It is therefore avoided in newborns.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol accumulates in neonates (immature glucuronidation) causing gray baby syndrome.

questions.text: Linezolid is mainly used for:
questions.explanation: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone active against resistant gram-positive organisms including MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci, and it can be given orally. It has essentially no gram-negative or antipseudomonal activity.
questions.keyConcept: Linezolid: oral option for MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

questions.text: Prolonged use of linezolid can cause which serious adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Linezolid can cause reversible myelosuppression, most notably thrombocytopenia, with courses beyond about two weeks, so blood counts must be monitored. It is also a weak MAO inhibitor risking serotonin syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Prolonged linezolid causes thrombocytopenia/myelosuppression (monitor CBC).

questions.text: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8 years and in pregnancy because they cause:
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines chelate calcium in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent yellow-brown tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth. This is why they are avoided in young children and pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracyclines chelate calcium - tooth discoloration and bone growth depression; avoid <8y/pregnancy.
options: Discoloration of teeth and depression of bone growth

questions.text: The antibiotic most commonly associated with pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile is:
questions.explanation: Clindamycin is classically linked to C. difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis because it strongly suppresses normal colonic flora. Vancomycin is in fact a treatment for this condition.
questions.keyConcept: Clindamycin is the classic cause of C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.text: The antibiotic of choice in hepatic coma or portal-systemic encephalopathy is:
questions.explanation: Neomycin is given orally to suppress ammonia-producing intestinal bacteria in hepatic coma because it is poorly absorbed systemically. The other antibiotics are not used for this gut-decontamination indication.
questions.keyConcept: Oral neomycin lowers ammonia production in hepatic coma.

questions.text: The following is NOT a therapeutic use of aminoglycosides:
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides are ineffective against anaerobes because uptake requires oxygen, so anaerobic brain abscess is not a therapeutic use. They may be used for serious gram-negative UTIs, synergistically in endocarditis, and selected intra-abdominal infections with appropriate partners.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides do not treat anaerobic infections.

questions.text: The main reason for the limited use of chloramphenicol is the high incidence of:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is limited by potentially fatal idiosyncratic aplastic anemia, in addition to reversible dose-related marrow suppression. Hepatotoxicity, interstitial nephritis and pulmonary fibrosis are not its limiting hallmark toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol use is limited mainly by aplastic anemia.

questions.text: The two most important dose-related toxicities of aminoglycosides are:
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides accumulate in renal tubular cells and cochlear/vestibular hair cells, producing dose-related nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Monitoring levels and once-daily dosing reduce these risks.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are the key dose-related toxicities.

questions.text: Tigecycline, a glycylcycline related to the tetracyclines, is notable for:
questions.explanation: Tigecycline has a broad spectrum including many multidrug-resistant gram-positive and gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, and evades common tetracycline resistance. Like tetracyclines it binds the 30S subunit, is given IV, and is avoided in pregnancy/children.
questions.keyConcept: Tigecycline: broad MDR coverage; IV only; shares tetracycline class cautions.

questions.text: Which agent is most effective in treatment of Rickettsia, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia infections?
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines, especially doxycycline, are highly effective against intracellular and atypical organisms such as rickettsiae, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia. Vancomycin and penicillin target cell walls and gentamicin is ineffective for these intracellular/atypical organisms.
questions.keyConcept: Doxycycline/tetracyclines cover rickettsiae, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia.

questions.text: Which antibiotic is most likely to cause aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol causes a rare, dose-independent, idiosyncratic aplastic anemia in addition to dose-dependent reversible marrow suppression. This serious toxicity restricts its use to life-threatening infections.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol causes idiosyncratic aplastic anemia and dose-related marrow suppression.

questions.text: Which antibiotic is used orally to reduce ammonia-producing gut flora in hepatic coma?
questions.explanation: Neomycin is too toxic for systemic use but, being poorly absorbed, is given orally to suppress ammonia-forming colonic bacteria in hepatic encephalopathy. The other agents are not used for this purpose.
questions.keyConcept: Oral neomycin reduces gut flora/ammonia in hepatic coma.

questions.text: Which drug/mechanism match is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Gentamicin binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, not 50S. Daptomycin disrupts the cell membrane, macrolides inhibit 50S translocation, and quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase.
questions.keyConcept: Gentamicin is a 30S aminoglycoside; macrolides are 50S inhibitors.
options: Gentamycin / binds 50S and inhibits protein synthesis

questions.text: Which macrolide is a potent inhibitor of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, raising the levels of drugs like theophylline and warfarin?
questions.explanation: Erythromycin (and clarithromycin) strongly inhibit CYP3A4, increasing plasma levels of theophylline, warfarin, carbamazepine and others. Azithromycin has minimal enzyme inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Erythromycin/clarithromycin inhibit CYP450; azithromycin does not.

questions.text: Which of the following is untrue about aminoglycosides?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides require oxygen-dependent uptake, so they are ineffective against anaerobic bacteria. Their bactericidal concentration-dependent action and nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity are correct features.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides do not work against anaerobes because uptake requires oxygen.
options: They require oxygen-dependent transport into bacteria
They are effective against anaerobic infections
They may cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity

questions.text: Which of the following statements about chloramphenicol is correct?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol inhibits hepatic CYP enzymes, prolonging the effect of warfarin, phenytoin and other drugs. It binds the 50S subunit, is dangerous in neonates (gray baby syndrome) and is reserved for serious infections only.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol is a hepatic enzyme inhibitor (potentiates warfarin/phenytoin) and binds 50S.
options: It is the drug of first choice for most infections
It inhibits hepatic microsomal enzymes and can prolong the action of warfarin

questions.text: Which protein synthesis inhibitor binds the 50S ribosomal subunit?
questions.explanation: Macrolides such as erythromycin bind the 50S subunit and block translocation. Tetracyclines and aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin) act on the 30S subunit.
questions.keyConcept: 50S binders: macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid; 30S: tetracyclines, aminoglycosides.

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG about azithromycin?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin has minimal hepatic microsomal enzyme inhibition compared with erythromycin and clarithromycin, so C is wrong. It has better gram-negative activity than erythromycin, a long half-life and is useful for atypical pneumonia in children.
questions.keyConcept: Azithromycin has little CYP inhibition and a long half-life.
options: It is more effective on gram-negative organisms than erythromycin
It has a long half-life and is taken once daily
It is a hepatic microsomal enzyme inhibitor
It is used as an alternative to tetracyclines in mycoplasma pneumonia in children

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG about chloramphenicol?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits peptidyl transferase, so 30S binding is wrong. Its marrow toxicity, CNS penetration and anaerobic activity are correct teaching points.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol is a 50S inhibitor, not a 30S inhibitor.
options: Aplastic anemia is the most serious adverse effect
It can cross the BBB and is effective against anaerobic infections
It is used in brain abscess and bacterial meningitis
It binds with 30S bacterial ribosome leading to protein synthesis inhibition

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG about pharmacokinetics of tetracyclines?
questions.explanation: Bile duct obstruction and hepatic/renal dysfunction generally prolong doxycycline or tetracycline persistence rather than decrease half-life, so this statement is wrong. Cation chelation, poor CSF penetration and doxycycline's long-acting biliary profile are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracycline absorption falls with cations; doxycycline is long-acting and biliary excreted.
options: Antacids containing calcium decrease their absorption
They enter CSF in insufficient amount for therapeutic use
Doxycycline is long-acting, lipophilic, metabolized in the liver and excreted in bile
Bile duct obstruction, hepatic or renal dysfunction decrease their half-life

questions.text: Match each drug with its specific feature.
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and deposit in developing bones and teeth. Aminoglycosides concentrate in renal cortex and inner ear, rifampicin colors urine red-orange, and cefoperazone can cause hypoprothrombinemia with bleeding risk.
questions.keyConcept: Key drug features: tetracyclines teeth/bone, aminoglycosides kidney/ear, rifampicin red urine, cefoperazone bleeding.

pairs.target: Deposit in renal cortex and inner ear

questions.text: Match each tetracycline antibiotic with its most appropriate characteristic.
questions.explanation: Tetracycline is short acting, doxycycline is long acting with biliary excretion, minocycline is long acting and historically used for meningococcal carriers, and demeclocycline antagonizes ADH action in SIADH. This preserves the original matching relationship while using the updated ASU matching schema.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracycline subclass matching: tetracycline short acting, doxycycline biliary, minocycline carriers, demeclocycline SIADH.

pairs.target: Long acting and used in biliary infection
Long acting and used in meningococcal carriers
Used in syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion

questions.text: A drug used in resistant staphylococcal infection, tuberculosis and as part of first-choice brucellosis therapy is:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is used in tuberculosis, can be combined for resistant staphylococcal infections, and is combined with doxycycline in brucellosis. Gentamicin, daptomycin and vancomycin do not cover this full set of indications.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin: TB, selected resistant staph combinations, and brucellosis with doxycycline.

questions.text: A female patient diagnosed with tuberculosis is taking a drug that may seriously decrease plasma levels of concomitantly used drugs. Which drug is it?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent hepatic microsomal enzyme inducer and can lower plasma levels of many co-administered drugs, including oral contraceptives, warfarin and antiepileptics. Ciprofloxacin is more associated with enzyme inhibition, not induction.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin decreases levels of many drugs via enzyme induction.

questions.text: A patient on rifampicin should be warned that the drug commonly causes:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin and its metabolites are colored and harmlessly stain body fluids orange-red, including urine, sweat and tears, and can permanently stain soft contact lenses. Patients should be reassured this is expected.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin turns body fluids orange-red (and stains contact lenses).
options: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat and tears

questions.text: A patient taking metronidazole develops severe nausea, vomiting and flushing after drinking alcohol. This is due to:
questions.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde accumulation and a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting) when alcohol is consumed. Patients must avoid alcohol during and shortly after therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Metronidazole + alcohol = disulfiram-like reaction (avoid alcohol).

questions.text: All the following are effective in anaerobic infection EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Gentamicin and other aminoglycosides require oxygen-dependent uptake and therefore are ineffective against anaerobes. Metronidazole, clinafloxacin and cefoxitin have anaerobic activity in the source teaching.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides are ineffective against anaerobes.

questions.text: All the following are true about rifampicin EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin actually penetrates the CSF and IS used in meningococcal/Haemophilus carrier prophylaxis and as part of meningitis-related regimens, so the statement that it is 'not used in meningitis' is false. Enzyme induction and orange-red secretions are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin is a strong CYP inducer; it does penetrate CSF and is used for carrier prophylaxis.
options: It is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
It is used in tuberculosis and for meningococcal carrier prophylaxis
It can cause orange-red discoloration of secretions
It is not used in meningitis

questions.text: All the following can treat infections with atypical organisms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Atypical organisms lack typical cell wall targets or are intracellular, so doxycycline, macrolides and respiratory fluoroquinolones are useful. Imipenem is a beta-lactam cell-wall inhibitor and is not used for atypical organisms.
questions.keyConcept: Atypical infections are treated with doxycycline, macrolides or respiratory fluoroquinolones, not beta-lactams.

questions.text: Because rifampicin strongly induces hepatic enzymes, it can reduce the effectiveness of:
questions.explanation: As a potent CYP450 inducer, rifampicin accelerates the metabolism of oral contraceptives, warfarin, anticonvulsants, antiretrovirals and many other drugs, reducing their efficacy. Dose adjustments or alternative contraception are needed.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin's enzyme induction lowers levels of OCPs, warfarin and many drugs.
options: Oral contraceptives, warfarin and many other drugs

questions.text: Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in children and pregnancy because they cause:
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones can damage growing cartilage and are associated with tendinitis and tendon rupture, so they are generally avoided in children and pregnancy. Tooth discoloration is a tetracycline effect.
questions.keyConcept: Fluoroquinolones damage cartilage and tendons - caution in children/pregnancy.

questions.text: Fluoroquinolones can prolong which ECG interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones (notably moxifloxacin) can prolong the QT interval and predispose to torsades de pointes, so caution is needed with other QT-prolonging drugs and in patients with electrolyte disturbance. The other intervals are not characteristically affected.
questions.keyConcept: Fluoroquinolones prolong the QT interval (torsades risk).

questions.text: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin act by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA supercoiling and replication, which is bactericidal. RNA polymerase is the target of rifampicin and folate enzymes are targeted by sulfonamides/trimethoprim.
questions.keyConcept: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase (topo II) and topoisomerase IV.
options: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV

questions.text: Metronidazole is the drug of choice for:
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is activated within anaerobic organisms to form reactive intermediates that damage DNA, making it highly effective against anaerobes and protozoa such as Entamoeba and Giardia. It has no activity against aerobes.
questions.keyConcept: Metronidazole covers anaerobes and protozoa (amoeba, Giardia, Trichomonas).
options: Anaerobic infections and certain protozoa (e.g. amoebiasis, giardiasis)

questions.text: One adverse effect of rifampicin is:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin can cause rash and hypersensitivity reactions in addition to hepatotoxicity and orange-red secretions. Gout is linked to pyrazinamide, neuropathy to isoniazid and visual disturbance to ethambutol.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin adverse effects include rash, hepatotoxicity and orange-red body fluids.

questions.text: Oral absorption of ciprofloxacin is reduced by co-administration with:
questions.explanation: Like tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones chelate di- and trivalent cations, so antacids, iron, calcium and similar products markedly reduce their absorption. Dosing should be separated from these agents.
questions.keyConcept: Cations/antacids chelate fluoroquinolones and reduce absorption.

questions.text: Prolonged QT interval is commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: The source key links QT prolongation to norfloxacin and erythromycin. Doxycycline is not a typical QT-prolonging antibiotic.
questions.keyConcept: Macrolides and some quinolones can prolong QT interval.

questions.text: Rifampicin inhibits which bacterial enzyme?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin binds and inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking the initiation of mRNA synthesis. This selective action does not affect the structurally different human enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

questions.text: The following is NOT an indication for rifampicin:
questions.explanation: The source key marks meningitis case as not an indication for rifampicin. Rifampicin is used in tuberculosis, in selected resistant staphylococcal combinations, and with doxycycline for brucellosis.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin is core TB therapy and combines in brucellosis; source flags meningitis case as not an indication.

questions.text: The following is a WRONG statement:
questions.explanation: Ciprofloxacin is not reliable for MRSA or anaerobic infections, so this statement is wrong. Neomycin's oral local use, macrolide safety alternatives, and chloramphenicol enzyme inhibition are correct teaching points.
questions.keyConcept: Ciprofloxacin is not an MRSA/anaerobe drug.
options: Neomycin is not absorbed orally and is used as intestinal antiseptic before surgery
Macrolides are alternatives to penicillins and tetracyclines in children and pregnancy
Chloramphenicol is highly lipophilic and acts as a hepatic microsomal enzyme inhibitor
Ciprofloxacin is effective in MRSA and anaerobic infections

questions.text: Together with oral vancomycin, which drug is a first-line treatment for Clostridioides difficile pseudomembranous colitis?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is effective against C. difficile and has long been used (with oral vancomycin) to treat pseudomembranous colitis. Its anaerobic activity targets the toxin-producing organism.
questions.keyConcept: C. difficile colitis is treated with oral vancomycin or metronidazole.

questions.text: Which drug or drugs should be avoided with dairy products or antacids?
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines and ciprofloxacin chelate divalent/trivalent cations in dairy products and antacids, markedly reducing absorption. Erythromycin is not primarily limited by this chelation interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones chelate calcium/magnesium/iron, reducing absorption.

questions.text: Which fluoroquinolone is preferred (a 'respiratory fluoroquinolone') for community-acquired pneumonia due to its enhanced activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: Levofloxacin (and moxifloxacin) are respiratory fluoroquinolones with strong activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae, making them suitable for community-acquired pneumonia. Ciprofloxacin has comparatively weak pneumococcal activity, and norfloxacin/nalidixic acid are limited to the urinary tract.
questions.keyConcept: Levofloxacin/moxifloxacin = respiratory fluoroquinolones for CAP.

questions.text: Which quinolone match is/are best treated by the named quinolone member?
questions.explanation: The source key accepts clinafloxacin for anaerobes and levofloxacin for atypical pneumonia. Pseudomonas is better associated with ciprofloxacin than levofloxacin, so B is not accepted.
questions.keyConcept: Clinafloxacin covers anaerobes; levofloxacin covers respiratory atypicals; ciprofloxacin is stronger for Pseudomonas.

questions.text: Which statement concerning quinolones is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Quinolones are concentration-dependent bactericidal antibiotics with a post-antibiotic effect, so saying they are time-dependent is wrong. QT prolongation and the listed spectrum/use statements match the source teaching.
questions.keyConcept: Quinolones are concentration-dependent, not time-dependent.
options: Ciprofloxacin is of choice in typhoid fever

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG about quinolones?
questions.explanation: Quinolones can cause CNS adverse effects such as dizziness, insomnia and seizures; saying they have no CNS adverse effects is wrong. Antacids reduce absorption, levofloxacin is respiratory, and ciprofloxacin is used for infective diarrhea and Pseudomonas.
questions.keyConcept: Fluoroquinolones have CNS adverse effects and chelate with antacids.
options: Levofloxacin is effective in respiratory tract infection including atypical pneumonia
They cannot cross the BBB and have no CNS adverse effects
Ciprofloxacin is used empirically in infective diarrhea and Pseudomonas infection

questions.text: Which urinary antiseptic quinolone has no useful systemic antibacterial activity and is used only for urinary tract infections?
questions.explanation: Nalidixic acid is a first-generation (non-fluorinated) quinolone that reaches antibacterial levels only in urine, so it is used solely as a urinary antiseptic. The fluoroquinolones listed achieve systemic concentrations.
questions.keyConcept: Nalidixic acid = urinary-only quinolone (no systemic activity).

questions.text: A patient stabilized on warfarin develops bleeding after starting which antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole (the sulfonamide component) inhibits warfarin metabolism and displaces it from plasma protein, raising free warfarin levels and causing bleeding. The INR must be monitored closely.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole potentiates warfarin (enzyme inhibition + protein displacement) - bleeding risk.

questions.text: A serious dermatologic adverse effect associated with sulfonamides is:
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides are an important cause of severe hypersensitivity skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Patients should stop the drug at the first sign of rash.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN.

questions.text: All the following are adverse effects of co-trimoxazole EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole can cause sulfonamide-related kernicterus, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Red man syndrome is caused by rapid vancomycin infusion, not co-trimoxazole.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole causes sulfonamide toxicities; red man syndrome is vancomycin.

questions.text: Co-trimoxazole is the combination of:
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole combines sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, producing sequential blockade of two steps in folate synthesis for a synergistic bactericidal effect. This pairing matches the half-lives of the two drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole = sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim (sequential folate blockade).

questions.text: Co-trimoxazole is the drug of choice for prophylaxis and treatment of which opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients?
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is first-line for both prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, a common opportunistic infection in HIV and other immunocompromised patients. The other infections require different agents.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole = drug of choice for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

questions.text: In co-trimoxazole, sulfonamide is combined with:
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole combines sulfamethoxazole, a sulfonamide, with trimethoprim to block sequential steps in folate synthesis. This produces synergistic antibacterial activity.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole = sulfonamide + trimethoprim.

questions.text: Sulfonamides can precipitate hemolysis in patients with which enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides are oxidant drugs and can cause acute hemolytic anemia in patients with G6PD deficiency, who cannot protect red cells from oxidative stress. They should be avoided in such patients.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (oxidant stress).

questions.text: Sulfonamides exert their antibacterial effect by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides are structural analogues of PABA and competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking bacterial folate synthesis. Humans obtain preformed folate from the diet, giving selective toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase (compete with PABA).
options: Dihydropteroate synthase (PABA incorporation into folic acid)

questions.text: Sulfonamides given near term or to neonates can cause kernicterus because they:
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin-binding sites; in neonates the freed bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier and can cause kernicterus. They are therefore avoided in late pregnancy and the newborn.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin - kernicterus risk in neonates.

questions.text: The following is NOT a therapeutic use for co-trimoxazole:
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is used for urinary and respiratory infections and may be used for some community MRSA infections, but it is not a standard treatment for meningitis. Meningitis requires agents with reliable CSF penetration and organism-specific activity.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole is not a standard meningitis drug.

questions.text: To reduce the risk of crystalluria with older sulfonamides, patients are advised to:
questions.explanation: Older, poorly soluble sulfonamides can crystallize in acidic urine and cause crystalluria; adequate hydration and urinary alkalinization keep them soluble and protect the kidneys. Fluid restriction would worsen the risk.
questions.keyConcept: Prevent sulfonamide crystalluria with high fluids and urine alkalinization.
options: Maintain a high fluid intake and alkalinize the urine

questions.text: Trimethoprim acts by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim selectively inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, a step downstream of the sulfonamide target, blocking conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. The sequential blockade with a sulfonamide is synergistic.
questions.keyConcept: Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase (synergy with sulfonamides).

questions.text: Which statement is WRONG about co-trimoxazole?
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is unsafe in newborns because of kernicterus risk and unsafe in favism/G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis risk, so D is wrong. The combination and synergy statements are correct, and it can have activity against some MRSA strains in the source teaching.
questions.keyConcept: Avoid co-trimoxazole in neonates and G6PD deficiency.
options: It is a combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim
It is a synergistic combination with wider spectrum
It is safe in newborns and favism

questions.text: A patient develops severe watery diarrhea, fever and abdominal pain, and Clostridioides difficile infection is confirmed. The antimicrobial therapy is:
questions.explanation: Antibiotic-associated C. difficile colitis is treated with oral vancomycin or metronidazole in the source-keyed item. Amoxicillin may precipitate antibiotic-associated diarrhea rather than treat it, while both B and C are therapeutic options.
questions.keyConcept: C. difficile colitis is treated with oral vancomycin or metronidazole.

questions.text: A patient on long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics develops oral and vaginal candidiasis. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress normal bacterial flora, allowing overgrowth of resistant organisms or fungi such as Candida - a superinfection. This is distinct from allergy or direct toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Broad-spectrum antibiotics cause superinfection (e.g. Candida) by suppressing normal flora.
options: A superinfection due to suppression of normal flora

questions.text: A patient with G6PD deficiency develops typhoid fever. Which is the best antibiotic choice?
questions.explanation: In G6PD deficiency the oxidant drugs co-trimoxazole, chloramphenicol and nitrofurantoin can trigger hemolysis, so they are avoided. Amoxicillin is effective in typhoid fever and does not provoke hemolysis, making it the safest choice.
questions.keyConcept: In G6PD deficiency choose amoxicillin for typhoid; avoid oxidant drugs (sulfa, chloramphenicol, nitrofurantoin).

questions.text: A patient with Pseudomonas infection is receiving IV gentamycin with unsatisfactory response. If penicillin is administered in a separate IV line, what will occur?
questions.explanation: A cell-wall-active penicillin facilitates aminoglycoside penetration into bacteria, producing synergistic killing when given separately to avoid physical inactivation. The key effect is enhanced antibacterial response, not chemical neutralization or nephrotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin plus aminoglycoside can be synergistic when administered separately.
options: Chemical neutralization and abolishment of penicillin effect
Colitis due to superinfection may develop
Penicillin will enhance the bacterial response to the aminoglycoside

questions.text: A patient with a serious MRSA infection resistant to vancomycin needs parenteral therapy (non-pulmonary). A suitable IM/IV agent is:
questions.explanation: Daptomycin is a parenteral bactericidal lipopeptide effective against MRSA and vancomycin-resistant gram-positive organisms, suitable for bacteremia and skin/soft-tissue infection. It cannot be used for pneumonia because surfactant inactivates it.
questions.keyConcept: Daptomycin: parenteral option for resistant gram-positives (not pneumonia).

questions.text: A patient with a serious MRSA infection that is also resistant to vancomycin can be treated orally with:
questions.explanation: Linezolid is active against MRSA and vancomycin-resistant gram-positive organisms and has excellent oral bioavailability, making it an oral option in this scenario. Beta-lactams and gentamicin are ineffective against MRSA.
questions.keyConcept: Linezolid: oral agent for vancomycin-resistant MRSA.

questions.text: A patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia and a documented penicillin allergy is best treated with which oral/IV agent active against typical and atypical pathogens?
questions.explanation: A respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae plus atypical organisms and is safe in penicillin allergy, making it ideal for community-acquired pneumonia. Gentamicin and metronidazole lack the needed respiratory-pathogen coverage.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory fluoroquinolones cover CAP (typical + atypical) and are safe in penicillin allergy.

questions.text: A pregnant woman with G6PD deficiency needs oral treatment for typhoid fever. The most appropriate antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: Ampicillin is safe in pregnancy, does not cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and is effective orally against typhoid. Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy, while co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol are oxidant/unsafe in this setting.
questions.keyConcept: Ampicillin: safe oral typhoid therapy in pregnancy and G6PD deficiency.

questions.text: A young woman develops an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. An appropriate first-line oral agent is:
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated cystitis is treated with oral agents that concentrate in urine such as nitrofurantoin or co-trimoxazole. Vancomycin and benzathine penicillin do not target typical uropathogens, and gentamicin is parenteral and reserved for more serious infection.
questions.keyConcept: Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin or co-trimoxazole first-line.

questions.text: Antibacterial-associated colitis is not likely to occur with:
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is used to treat C. difficile-associated colitis, so it is least likely among these to be considered a cause in the source set. Clindamycin is the classic precipitating antibiotic.
