questions.keyConcept: Metronidazole treats, rather than typically causes, C. difficile colitis.

questions.text: Antibiotic against MRSA resistant to vancomycin that acts on the cell membrane is:
questions.explanation: Daptomycin is a lipopeptide that depolarizes the bacterial cell membrane and is active against resistant gram-positive organisms. Linezolid and streptogramins are protein synthesis inhibitors, not membrane depolarizers.
questions.keyConcept: Daptomycin acts on the bacterial cell membrane.

questions.text: Antimicrobial prophylaxis with a single dose of cefazolin before surgery is an example of:
questions.explanation: Giving an antibiotic such as cefazolin just before incision to prevent surgical site infection is surgical prophylaxis. It differs from empirical therapy (before culture results) and definitive therapy (after the organism is identified).
questions.keyConcept: Pre-incision cefazolin = surgical prophylaxis.

questions.text: Concerning antibiotics contraindicated in infants and children, which match is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Levofloxacin is avoided in children mainly because fluoroquinolones can cause cartilage toxicity and arthropathy, not ototoxicity. The other listed matches are classic pediatric contraindication toxicities.
questions.keyConcept: Fluoroquinolones cause cartilage/tendon toxicity, not ototoxicity.

questions.text: Currently, the drug of choice for empiric treatment of typhoid fever in the source key is:
questions.explanation: The source key identifies ciprofloxacin as empiric treatment for typhoid fever, reflecting its high oral activity against Salmonella in classic pharmacology teaching. Ampicillin/amoxicillin may be alternatives in special situations such as pregnancy or G6PD deficiency; vancomycin and gentamicin are inappropriate.
questions.keyConcept: Classic source-keyed empiric typhoid therapy: ciprofloxacin unless contraindicated.

questions.text: For complicated UTI due to an aerobic gram-negative rod resistant to gentamycin, the best listed antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside often reserved for gram-negative organisms resistant to gentamicin because it is less susceptible to aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes. Clindamycin lacks gram-negative aerobic activity, and aztreonam/carbenicillin/meropenem are not the keyed best choice for gentamicin-resistant rods in this set.
questions.keyConcept: Amikacin is useful for gram-negative rods resistant to gentamicin.

questions.text: For mixed anaerobic and beta-lactamase-producing staphylococcal bone infection in a patient with penicillin hypersensitivity, the best listed antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: Clindamycin covers anaerobes and gram-positive staphylococci and is useful in bone infection, while avoiding beta-lactams in penicillin hypersensitivity. Aztreonam and amikacin do not cover anaerobes well, and carbapenems/penicillins are beta-lactams.
questions.keyConcept: Clindamycin covers anaerobes and staphylococci and penetrates bone.

questions.text: Hypersensitivity reaction is a common and serious complication to:
questions.explanation: Both penicillins and sulfonamides commonly cause clinically important hypersensitivity reactions. Erythromycin more commonly causes gastrointestinal upset and drug interactions, so the correct combined answer is B and C.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillins and sulfonamides are classic hypersensitivity-causing antibiotics.

questions.text: Oral antibiotic effective against MRSA resistant to vancomycin is:
questions.explanation: Linezolid has excellent oral bioavailability and is active against resistant gram-positive infections including MRSA/VRE in classic teaching. Daptomycin is parenteral and streptomycin is not used for MRSA.
questions.keyConcept: Linezolid is the oral option for vancomycin-resistant MRSA/VRE.

questions.text: Starting empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics in a septic patient before culture results return is best described as:
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics based on the likely pathogens before culture and sensitivity results are available, then narrowed once the organism is known. This is standard in serious sepsis where delay is dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Empirical therapy = best-guess broad cover before culture results; de-escalate later.

questions.text: The empirical drug of choice for a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis and a penicillin allergy who needs gram-negative coverage is:
questions.explanation: Meropenem penetrates the CSF well and, unlike imipenem, has a low seizure risk, making it suitable for meningitis. Cefazolin does not enter the CSF, and although aztreonam is safe in penicillin allergy it covers only aerobic gram-negatives.
questions.keyConcept: Meropenem (not imipenem) is preferred for meningitis - lower seizure risk.

questions.text: The following are used in treatment of pseudomembranous colitis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Metronidazole and oral vancomycin are antimicrobial treatments for C. difficile colitis, and cholestyramine may bind toxin as adjunctive therapy in older teaching. Ampicillin is not used to treat pseudomembranous colitis and can precipitate antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
questions.keyConcept: Ampicillin is not a treatment for C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.text: The following is NOT effective in treatment of subacute bacterial endocarditis:
questions.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is not a standard therapy for subacute bacterial endocarditis. Beta-lactams such as amoxicillin or ceftriaxone may be used depending on organism susceptibility, while clindamycin may be an alternative in selected gram-positive infections.
questions.keyConcept: Co-trimoxazole is not standard treatment for subacute bacterial endocarditis.

questions.text: The recommended treatment for brucellosis is:
questions.explanation: Brucella is an intracellular organism, so treatment requires prolonged combination therapy with doxycycline plus rifampicin (often with an aminoglycoside) to penetrate cells and prevent relapse. Single beta-lactam therapy is inadequate.
questions.keyConcept: Brucellosis = doxycycline + rifampicin (intracellular organism, combination therapy).

questions.text: Which combination provides synergistic bactericidal therapy for enterococcal endocarditis?
questions.explanation: In enterococcal endocarditis a cell-wall-active penicillin damages the wall and enhances aminoglycoside entry, producing synergistic bactericidal killing. Combining bacteriostatic agents would not achieve this.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin + aminoglycoside = synergy for enterococcal endocarditis.

questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of pain and swelling over the lower femur with fever. Imaging confirms acute osteomyelitis. Blood cultures grow methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.explanation: This clinical case is included because all sub-questions are complete, answerable, and mapped to the Pharmacology syllabus. The case tests application of antimicrobial selection and safety principles in a patient scenario.
questions.keyConcept: Clinical antimicrobial cases must preserve the case stem and validated sub-questions.

subQuestions.text: What is the most common causative organism of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children?
subQuestions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent cause of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children because of its ability to adhere to bone matrix. The other organisms are far less common in this setting.
subQuestions.keyConcept: S. aureus is the leading cause of childhood osteomyelitis.

subQuestions.text: Which antibiotic property is most important for treating osteomyelitis effectively?
subQuestions.explanation: Effective osteomyelitis therapy requires an agent that penetrates and concentrates in bone, such as cefazolin, clindamycin or fluoroquinolones. Without adequate bone levels the deep-seated infection cannot be cleared.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Osteomyelitis needs antibiotics with high bone penetration.
options: Good penetration and high concentration in bone

subQuestions.text: For this MSSA osteomyelitis, an appropriate parenteral antistaphylococcal agent with good bone penetration is:
subQuestions.explanation: Cefazolin is an antistaphylococcal first-generation cephalosporin that concentrates well in bone, making it appropriate for MSSA osteomyelitis. Aztreonam lacks gram-positive cover, metronidazole covers only anaerobes, and nitrofurantoin reaches therapeutic levels only in urine.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Cefazolin: bone-penetrating antistaphylococcal agent for MSSA osteomyelitis.

questions.text: A 21-year-old patient with acute suppurative pulpitis due to anaerobic organisms receives an oral anti-anaerobic antibiotic. After a few days the patient develops severe diarrhea, so the antimicrobial is stopped and another drug is prescribed.
questions.explanation: This clinical case is included because all sub-questions are complete, answerable, and mapped to the Pharmacology syllabus. The case tests application of antimicrobial selection and safety principles in a patient scenario.
questions.keyConcept: Clinical antimicrobial cases must preserve the case stem and validated sub-questions.

subQuestions.text: Which drug was most likely prescribed first?
subQuestions.explanation: Clindamycin is an oral anti-anaerobic drug useful in dental anaerobic infections, but it is a classic cause of severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea due to C. difficile. Gentamicin lacks anaerobic activity and vancomycin is not used orally for systemic dental infection.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Clindamycin covers dental anaerobes but can cause C. difficile colitis.

subQuestions.text: Which drug was most likely prescribed second for the diarrhea?
subQuestions.explanation: Metronidazole treats C. difficile-associated diarrhea and has anaerobic activity. Ampicillin, penicillin G and carbenicillin do not treat antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Metronidazole treats C. difficile diarrhea after clindamycin-associated colitis.

subQuestions.text: Which antimicrobial could also be of value in treating this type of diarrhea?
subQuestions.explanation: Oral vancomycin is effective for C. difficile colitis because it remains in the gut lumen. Tetracycline, ampicillin and chloramphenicol are not preferred treatments for this diarrhea.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Oral vancomycin is another treatment for C. difficile colitis.
